#4815. Why Your Most Original Colleague Can't Get Anything Done

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

Most teams have someone who thinks a bit differently. Many effective teams have a few. Sometimes that's good and sometimes it causes serious problems.

In a brainstorm, they might produce ten ideas while everyone else is still wondering how to structure their thoughts, or waiting to see what others say. Some are brilliant, some are baffling, or a combination of the two. They dress a little differently, follow their own passions unashamedly, and have a habit of questioning things everyone else doesn't notice or doesn't care to notice anymore.

In the right environment, and with some self-awareness and empathy, they can be the most interesting person in the room. They can also be the most frustrating, because despite a lot of good ideas, none of those ideas turns into reality. They have big ideas that they would love to see implemented by other people.

The unconventional style is one way of describing one of the "dark side" personality styles: everyday patterns that can help or hinder us at work, depending on how strongly they show up and where. Its extreme form resembles a clinical pattern of eccentric thinking and unusual perceptions. Most people with an unconventional style are nowhere near that. They simply have their own unique approach to life.

They tend to rely on their own understanding of how the world works, and it is often a rich, intense, and sometimes quirky one. For some, being different is unconscious. For others, it is a deliberate avoidance of anything conventional or ordinary. Either way, they are unlikely to change it to suit other people.

At their best, people with this style are interesting, different, and fun to be around. They are abstract and creative thinkers, and they can be remarkably tenacious, pursuing an idea long after others have given up, often with very little support.

They also perform an important function in teams. When everyone shares the same assumptions, they are the outsider on the inside. They ask the question that nobody else thought to ask, or offer an approach that breaks a deadlock. Think of the trainer whose odd analogy is the one that finally makes a complicated process click for a struggling new starter, or the analyst who notices that a problem everyone has been solving the same way for years could be approached from a completely different angle. A team without anyone like this risks drifting into comfortable groupthink.

There is evidence that unusual thinking and creativity overlap, but it is more nuanced than the stereotype of the eccentric genius. A meta-analysis by Acar and Sen (2013), combining results from 45 studies, found only a small overall link between creativity and personality dimensions that capture unusual perceptions, magical thinking, and eccentricity. However, there is some evidence that those who tend to experience life imaginatively and unusually can also be more creative.

The ability to put unconventional ideas into practice, though, can be more challenging, and the link with productivity is even more difficult to achieve.

The downside of this personality style is rarely a lack of ideas. The problem for team members is often the lack of follow-through. When someone's energy isn't channelled effectively, unconventional people can have lots of ideas, but nothing gets off the ground.

They can be easily distracted, drawn off on tangents, and quickly bored by tasks that don't fit their view of the world. Often, the routine parts of a project, such as documenting ideas, updating progress trackers, following templates, and managing a project through to completion, can feel unbearable. They can also be stubborn or disruptive when things don't go according to their plans, preferring their own way of doing things even when the team has agreed on another.

There is a social cost as well. People who are seen as eccentric are not always taken seriously, even when they are right. As I discussed in a post on how people enable dysfunction at work, the unconventional colleague may see a problem clearly but struggle to gain traction, because their protests are easily dismissed as another eccentric idea.

Distance can make this worse. In a remote team, the unconventional colleague can drift further into their own projects without anyone noticing until a deadline arrives. Left alone and out of the loop, people with this style can quickly spin off into their own world, building something fascinating that nobody asked for. In this case, the right adjustment is not stricter control, which they will resist, but more regular contact to make sure their passion and energy are pointed at the right target.

None of this means they lack motivation. As with people who are lower in conscientiousness, the motivation is there, but it may be challenging for them to apply it to the right priorities and connect with what the rest of the team needs to be productive.

Unconventional people can be successful, but they will be most effective in a workplace where people accept their quirks, and where they in turn make some effort to fit in and build relationships based on mutual respect. That works in both directions:

When they meet others halfway and align their talents with the team's priorities, unconventional people can be fun, vibrant, productive and innovative colleagues.

In a workplace, the challenge may be to direct that energy productively and prosocially. Part of doing that may mean remembering that they have plenty of time to pursue other creative pursuits outside of work.

Acar, S., & Sen, S. (2013). A multilevel meta-analysis of the relationship between creativity and schizotypy. Psychology of Aesthetics, Creativity, and the Arts, 7(3), 214–228. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0031975

MacRae, I. (2022). Dark social: Understanding the darker side of work, personality and social media. Bloomsbury.

#4814. Functional Core Workouts Are the Key to Moving Better in and Out of the Gym

Add these 15 expert-approved exercises into your weekly routine.

I don’t know about you, but doing core exercises is my least favorite part of workouts. Unfortunately, though, neglecting functional core training can make a big difference in your total-body strength, and how you move day to day.

Functional training focuses on compound movements that engage multiple muscle groups simultaneously and mimic the way our bodies move during everyday activities. Functionally training the core, specifically, involves strengthening the abdominal muscles that attach to the pelvis or spine.

For instance, a farmer’s carry mirrors the movement of carrying grocery bags. “This is an example of ‘bracing and carrying,’ where you need to keep a tight, braced core to carry the heavy weight,” says Corrine Carnation, CPT, a personal and group trainer at Equinox and creator of the Better You, Better Living program. Plus, a weak core can lead to poor posture and an increased risk of injury.

But the benefits extend way beyond preparing your body for real-life activities and protecting against pain or injury—keep reading for all the reasons you should do functional core movements.

Meet the experts: Corrine Carnation, CPT, is a personal and group trainer at Equinox. Cori Ritchey, CSCS, is the fitness editor at Women's Health, as well as a certified strength and conditioning coach and group fitness instructor in New York City.

Time: 30 minutes | Equipment (optional): kettlebell, dumbbells, slam ball, resistance band, or Pilates ring | Good for: core, hips, back

Instructions: Choose 5 to 6 exercises from the list below. Complete 2 to 3 sets of the indicated number of reps for each move. Aim to integrate functional core exercises into your training routine once or twice a week.

As these exercises become easier with practice, challenge yourself by increasing resistance while slightly decreasing the number of reps. For example, if 3 sets of 10 reps using bodyweight alone feels easy, try adding a weight or resistance band for 2 or 3 sets of 8 reps. By the last rep of each set, you should feel ready to stop but not completely at failure. When in doubt, start with bodyweight only, then add resistance until you feel the exercise is challenging, but doable.

Pro tip: Exercises aren’t one-size-fits-all, so it’s important to recognize when an exercise is either too challenging, too easy, or not comfortable for you. Keep in mind that every exercise can be modified if needed!

Why it rocks: The suitcase carry prepares the core for real-life activities such as carrying heavy things by your sides. It strengthens the core by making you resist the urge to bend, improving stability and balance—the added grip demand is a fun challenge, too.

1. Holding a weight in one hand, stand up tall and pull your shoulders back and down to prevent them from rolling forward. Keep your core tight and spine neutral.

2. Walk forward for 30 to 60 seconds while maintaining a strong grip and upright posture.

4. Turn around and pick the weight up again, this time with your left hand. Complete 4 reps on each side.

Why it rocks: The halo exercise improves shoulder mobility and stability while strengthening your core. Moving the weight around your head causes a perturbation (or distracting force) to your body, forcing you to stabilize using your core. This particular halo variation has the added benefit of enhancing upper-body strength, targeting the shoulders, back, and arms.

1. Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, holding one dumbbell in front of your chest with both hands and elbows bent at 90 degrees.

2. Slowly circle the dumbbell around your head, moving it clockwise from ear to ear, elbows hugging in.

3. Return to start and repeat the movement counterclockwise. That's 1 rep.

Why it rocks: Have you ever worried about straining your back when picking something up or twisting? This move strengthens the core, improves stability, and builds rotational strength to protect your body during these movements.

1. Sit on the floor with your knees bent and upper body leaned back until abs are engaged (aim for a 45-degree angle relative to the floor). Hold a slam ball or dumbbell close to your chest with your elbows bent.

2. Keeping your arms slightly bent, twist your torso to the left and slam the ball on the floor next to your left hip.

3. Twist your torso through center to the right and slam the ball on the floor near your right hip. That's 1 rep.

4. Continue alternating for a total of 10 to 12 reps.

Why it rocks: The overhead slam exercise requires you to stabilize your body as you lift and forcefully throw the ball down to the floor. It also strengthens your shoulders, arms, and upper back while improving explosive power and coordination.

1. Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart, a soft bend in knees, and core engaged, while holding a slam ball at your chest with both hands.

2. Rise up tall on your toes and extend your arms overhead holding the slam ball.

3. Bend at your hips (hinging forward slightly) and slam the ball on the floor directly in front of you. Exhale as you throw the ball down toward the floor with force. Be careful not to arch your back.

4. Catch the ball on the bounce while lowering back into the squat position. That's 1 rep.

Why it rocks: The wood chop exercise helps strengthen your core by working your abs and obliques, which can boost your twisting power and stability, building strength and coordination.

1. Start in a half-kneeling position with your left leg forward and your right leg back, both bent at 90 degrees, holding a dumbbell in front of your chest.

2. With your arms straight, torso upright, and hips facing forward, swiftly lower the weight diagonally across your body to the right hip while twisting to the right. Then, raise the weight to upper left diagonal while twisting to the left. That's 1 rep.

3. Complete 10 reps, then repeat on the other side.

Why it rocks: Keeping your lower back and head flush with the floor while your limbs shift weight will engage your deep core stabilizers. Being able to lift your legs and arms from this position is essential for a healthy spine.

1. Lie faceup holding one dumbbell horizontally in front of your chest with both hands. Lift legs to a tabletop position with your knees over hips, your lower back glued to the floor, and your core engaged.

2. Keeping one leg at a 90-degree angle, lower the other to tap your heel to the floor. As your leg lowers, reach your arms above your head to lower the weight toward the floor behind your head.

3. Engage your core to lift both your arms and leg back to start, then repeat on the opposite side. That's 1 rep.

Why it rocks: This exercise recruits your abdominal muscles to maintain balance and stability. A resistance band offers an added challenge for the core and lower body.

1. Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart and your hands on your hips or relaxed at your sides. (Optional: Place a resistance band around the arches of both feet.)

2. Balancing on one leg, draw one knee up toward your chest, hold for 1 second, then return it to the floor.

3. Repeat on the opposite side, alternating for 30 seconds. That’s 1 rep.

Why it rocks: Planks help you build the strength to push yourself up from the floor, which is important for many day-to-day activities. Adding the knee drive challenges your upper body and core to stabilize, improving your balance and coordination with uneven movements.

1. Start in a high plank position with your right foot lifted slightly up off the floor.

2. Exhale and pull your right knee toward your chest while rounding the spine to bring your nose toward your knee.

3. With control, reverse movement to return to plank position with right foot lifted. That's 1 rep.

Why it rocks: This exercise challenges you to sit up and lie down without using your hands, which requires strong core muscles. You can do it with a Pilates ring, a ball, or no equipment at all.

1. Lie faceup with your legs slightly bent, heels on floor, and arms extended straight above your head. (Optional: Place a mini resistance band around your wrists for an added challenge.)

2. Engage your core and draw your belly button in as you slowly begin to curl your spine off the mat one vertebra at a time. Roll up to an upright seated position while keeping biceps by the ears and arms reaching to the ceiling.

3. Once you reach the upright position, gradually reverse the movement by slowly rolling back down to the lying position. That's 1 rep.

Why it rocks: This exercise targets the glutes and core, the muscles needed to lift your hips. It's great for anyone who sits a lot, as it both strengthens and mobilizes the hips.

1. Lie faceup with knees bent and feet planted shoulder-width apart on the floor. Place your arms on the floor by your sides or for an added challenge, extend arms above with your hands directly above your shoulders and your palms facing in.

2. Engage your core as you press up into a glute bridge with your knees, hips, and shoulders in alignment, and hold this position.

3. From here, raise your right leg to a 90-degree angle, keeping the stationary leg firmly on the floor and pelvis stable. Return right foot to meet left foot in starting position. That’s 1 rep.

4. Continue alternating legs with your butt lifted and complete 10 to 12 reps on each side.

Why it rocks: The classic side plank targets the obliques, which are essential for stability and rotation in daily activities. It also works your shoulders and hips, promoting good posture and alignment.

1. Lie on your right side with your legs bent, your right elbow directly under your shoulder, and your left hand palm down.

2. Lift your hips off the mat, extending your legs to form a straight line from your head to heels.

3. Hold the position for 30 seconds, then repeat on the opposite side. That’s 1 rep.

Why it rocks: It's similar to the suitcase carry, but levels up the move a bit by testing your stabilization, as you have to stay upright even though the weight is trying to pull you down. Plus, it boosts your grip strength.

1. Stand up straight with feet shoulder-width apart and dumbbell in left hand.

2. Extend your right arm out to the side at a 45-degree angle from your body.

3. Slowly lift your left leg up until knee is at hip height.

4. Then, with control, lower your leg down to the floor. Repeat with right leg. That's 1 rep.

5. Complete 10 to 12 reps, then switch the dumbbell to your right hand.

Why it rocks: It targets your obliques, but also challenges your other core muscles in a more uncommon position. Additionally, it works your spinal mobility.

1. Kneel on left knee with toes pointed to the right, and right foot planted firmly to the side of body, holding a kettlebell in right hand.

2. Rack the kettlebell at chest, then lift it overhead, keeping eyes on the weight.

3. Slowly lower body down until left hand reaches the floor, then continue lowering until elbow and forearm reach the floor.

4. Reverse the movement with control and return to start. That's 1 rep.

Why it rocks: It's important to train rotation because we're constantly rotating in real life. Plank hip dips strengthen the obliques and stabilize the spine.

1. Start in a forearm plank position with elbows under shoulders and knees, hips, and torso in a straight line.

2. Drop right hip toward the floor, then return to center.

3. Immediately drop the left hip toward the floor.

Why it rocks: This move is one of the best for training functional power, and it demands stabilization from your core.

1. Stand with feet slightly wider than hip-width apart. Hold a kettlebell in front of your body with both hands, arms straight.

2. With a slight bend in the knees and a flat back, hinge at the hips and swing the kettlebell back through the legs. Use that momentum to stand and swing the kettlebell out in front of your body, up to shoulder height.

3. Thrust the hips forward and engage the glutes and core as you stand up straight. When the kettlebell hits shoulder height, the knees should be straight and glutes contracted in a full hip extension.

4. Allow the kettlebell to swing back down through the legs, while hinging at the hips. That's 1 rep.

The best functional core workouts include bodyweight and resistance exercises that challenge the core in different positions and directions. Your core is not one-dimensional, so it’s important to strengthen your body through movements that involve twisting, bending, and stabilizing in all directions. For example, a traditional situp only engages the core in a single plane of motion, but a workout with a Russian twist (for rotational movement), lateral side bends (for side-to-side movement), and plank variations (for multidirectional stability) ensures you are hitting your core muscles from all angles.

Carnation notes the importance of first activating your core before jumping right into a workout. To do so, she recommends the following: “Act as if someone is about to throw a basketball at your stomach.” It might sound odd, but this cue can be really effective in helping you tighten and brace your core to get ready for impact. It’s best to practice this abdominal bracing technique before going into more advanced exercises in order to ensure your core is engaged and ready for action, Carnation says.

Rachel Tavel is a doctor of physical therapy, strength and conditioning specialist certified by the National Strength and Conditioning Association, and writer. Her writing has been published in Forbes, Fortune, Men’s Health, Women’s Health, Runner’s World, SELF, Bicycling Magazine, The Huffington Post, and more. She co-authored the book “Stretch Yourself Healthy Guide: Easy Routines to Relieve Pain, Boost Energy, and Feel Refreshed” (Prevention, 2020) and is a Forbes Health Advisory Board Member. #4813. Andy Baraghani’s New NYC Restaurant is Full of Design Surprises

“I’ve always been obsessed with design, since I was a kid,” says Andy Baraghani. “I love how restaurant interiors can take you to a different place.”

At Ditto—the all-day café he is opening in New York’s Flatiron—the chef, cookbook author, and YouTube star has given that obsession free rein. With each design decision—from the vintage glass-prism Holophane pendants in the front window to the intense blue (tinted to match Benjamin Moore Buckland Blue) of the rear dining area’s Venetian plaster walls—he asked himself: “Would I actually do this in my home?” If the answer was yes, it passed the test.

The interior of Ditto, with Venetian plaster walls in a shade matching Benjamin Moore Buckland Blue, and Model S22 chairs from Galvanitas.

For Andy Baraghani, design is something of a family affair. His husband, Keith Pollock, is a former AD editor and now a West Elm executive. But opening a restaurant was never part of the plan. In fact, when Michael Silber, a restaurant investor behind New York hot spots like Borgo, Penny, and Bistrot Ha, approached him with the idea of a laid-back restaurant open for breakfast, lunch, and dinner, Baraghani admits his first reaction was: “I have no interest.”

It wasn’t for lack of experience. He had started his career in restaurants—from Chez Panisse in Berkeley, where he worked as a teenager, to Estela in New York—before becoming a food editor at Bon Appetit and winning a James Beard Award for his cookbook, The Cook You Want to Be.

But he bonded with Silber over their shared love of greenmarket cooking and decorating deep dives. When it came to Ditto, he says, he wanted the space to convey his personal style. It helped that he and Silber were on the same page. “Andy and I talked about styles ranging from Bauhaus, de Stijl, and classic modernism to 1970s and ’80s aesthetics from places like Italy and France,” Silber says.

They brought in like-minded collaborators: interior designer Eric Wink and architect Alta Indelman. Wink, a close friend of Baraghani who helped with the design of his and Pollock’s home, says the partners told him that New York’s much-missed City Bakery, which was two blocks uptown from Ditto’s 16th Street location, was an inspiration. “They wanted it to feel casual and approachable, with a bit of a New York diner quality,” Wink says.

Holophane pendant lamps hang in the restaurant’s front window.

The space, in a 1905 former factory (its last incarnation was an agnès b. store), is divided into three zones. In the front section, visitors can shop at a market area with hand-picked groceries. A glossy white counter with Bauhaus curves anchors the middle section; this is where customers line up, take a number, and either carry the food out or dine at laminate-topped tables under a trio of oversized custom fabric pendants. The menu, handwritten on a roll of butcher’s paper and updated daily, features dishes like pomegranate spoon salad and what Baraghani calls “the Platonic ideal of granola,” with tahini, maple syrup, and yogurt drizzled with fig-leaf oil.

The third zone, the one painted blue, features an open kitchen and café tables pulled up to a banquette that runs the length of the room. “There’s that good chaos in the middle and the back is a calmer moment,” says Baraghani.

Indelman, a veteran collaborator with New York restaurateurs like Andrew Tarlow and Gabe Stulman, was tasked with giving the space a utilitarian, high-tech ambience. She clad the walls and the open kitchen in patinated stainless steel and preserved industrial elements like structural arches and polished concrete floors.

But it was Baraghani and Silber who took the lead on honing the visual details of the interiors. “We went through 50 possibilities to find the right chair,” Silber says. The one they selected—a 1960s Dutch industrial chair, the Model S22 from Galvanitas—was sourced from Amsterdam Modern in Los Angeles.

Silber also spent hours on eBay bidding on midcentury ceramic bud vases. “They were each under $20 but put them together on a shelf and you have your own little Giorgio Morandi tableau,” he says.

White wall speakers and a French ceramic mask hang above the banquette, tables, and stools upholstered in Maharam’s Stripe It fabric.

The no-nonsense decor also features white wall speakers, created for the space by sound artist Tom Bloxam, and programmed with playlists created by Michael Scanlon of Chandelier Creative, which oversaw Ditto’s branding. But there are quirkier moments too. When it came to choosing fabric for the custom stools, Baraghani insisted on Maharam’s Stripe It, which he felt had a “Baja California” vibe. “We needed that twist,” he says. For his part, Wink specified his favorite stainless-steel toilet for the restrooms—Neo-Metro’s wall-mounted MiniLoo. “I added a custom wood top to soften it a bit,” Wink says.

Meanwhile, a pair of massive midcentury French ceramic faces that hang on a wall opposite the menu of the day are on loan from Baraghani’s own home. “They anchor the space and add a touch of craft,” he says. “I just knew they needed to be here.”

#4811. Gwyneth Paltrow Is Launching a New Podcast—Take the First Look Inside the “Goop Guide” Studio

Viewers tuning in to Gwyneth Paltrow’s new podcast, The Goop Guide, will be forgiven for assuming the show was filmed in a room inside her serene and stylish Montecito home. The setting for her new venture (launching on Netflix and Spotify November 11) upends the paradigm of a podcaster on a sofa next to a potted fern.

The Goop Guide is indeed recorded inside a studio, but Paltrow approached the space with just as much intention as her own home, enlisting interior designer Marie Carson to bring it to life. “I wanted it to feel like a beautiful, elevated nook of somebody’s old stone house somewhere,” Paltrow tells AD of the space.

“If we can’t be recording in my home, I want to give guests the feeling of comfort and coziness,” Paltrow says of her goal for the studio’s design.

The catch? Carson only had mere days to turn the sterile studio into something far cozier and conducive to the wide-ranging conversations Paltrow hoped to conduct during the show, which launches with Zoe Saldana as the first guest. “We started to decorate remotely and I looked at it and thought, This is not the direction,” Paltrow says of the space’s first iteration. “And so I called Marie and said, ‘We’re filming in, like, a week and I need you to come and fix this.’”

It wasn’t the tight timeline that initially gave Carson pause. “At first I said, ‘Oh my gosh, I’ve never done a set! What does that mean?’” recalls the designer. “But when Gwyneth said she wanted it to feel like a beautiful room in her home, I thought, Well, I can do that.” Previously, the two had collaborated on a space at Paltrow’s Brentwood property, which meant there was already a creative shorthand between them—incredibly helpful when they had only days to outfit the space before shooting commenced. “Gwyneth has such a strong direction of what she wants and such excellent taste,” Carson says. “So I was able to take her notes and run with it.”

The focal point for the studio’s design is a late-18th-century Flemish tapestry. “It added life to the space,” says Carson.

The Goop Kitchen founder wanted the focal point of the design to be a late-18th-century Flemish tapestry, whose landscape imagery features a palette of muted greens and taupes. “I thought it would be beautiful because of what they’ve lived through and what they’ve seen,” Paltrow says of tapestries. “I love them because you think about all the life going on in front of these things for hundreds and hundreds of years.” To complement the hanging, Carson added a 19th-century Belgian trestle table from Meg Turner Gallery, antique chairs reupholstered in Loro Piana brushed cashmere, and a handwoven hemp and silk rug sourced from Mansour. “Marie’s execution is flawless,” Paltrow says. “She has a real knack for finding the perfect thing that has the right dimensions and warmth.”

Paltrow commissioned a painting of magnolia from artist Rob Reynolds. The sconces are from Goop’s collection with CB2 and the wicker stools are from Galerie Provenence.

A close-up of one of the podcast chairs: an antique sourced from a shop in Pasadena and reupholstered with Loro Piana cashmere.

In the handful of shows Paltrow’s filmed so far, it appears her guests (which include Rick Rubin, Ke Huy Quan, and more) feel similarly at home. “Everyone who walks in is like, ‘I’ve done so many podcasts and I’ve never seen one like this! It feels like a real room and I feel so at ease.’’’ she says. Considering Paltrow will be filming dozens of episodes inside the space, she’s happy it’s comfortable for her as well. “I would definitely live in this room,” she says. “I think about this room all the time now when I’m not in it because I’m so obsessed with it.”

#4810. Who Knew Spirituality Might Prevent Addiction and Relapse?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

I have studied addiction from the laboratory bench to the bedside for more than 50 years. In that time, we’ve learned a great deal about addiction, withdrawal, craving, treatment, and relapse. And we now understand that dopamine, reward, stress, and some brain changes make quitting extremely difficult.

But what is the crux of addiction that makes it so difficult to treat? How do some people stop using while others relapse repeatedly, sometimes fatally?

Alcoholics Anonymous (A.A.) offered an answer long before neuroscientists could look at dopamine in the living brain. Putting a stop to drinking is only the beginning.

When Bill Wilson and Dr. Bob Smith founded Alcoholics Anonymous in 1935, they weren’t thinking about dopamine. They knew addiction and recovery from the patient's perspective. Nearly a century later, neuroscience is catching up. What A.A. called “spirituality” may involve measurable changes in thinking, behavior, social connections, and brain function. A.A. began with clinical observation and lived experience. Modern neuroscience is helping explain why recovery works.

Smith famously summarized A.A.’s core work as simply "love and service." Helping newcomers gives recovering individuals a sense of meaning, boosts self-efficacy (confidence in staying sober), and breaks the cycle of obsessive self-focus.

People might struggle to remember who and what they were before they developed a substance use disorder (SUD). Treatment is tough; it takes time, and people need persistence and resilience. With continued treatment, good things may then happen—relationships, accountability, purpose, and hope.

True, A.A. has spiritual roots, but it’s not a religion. A.A. members are encouraged to find a power greater than themselves. That may be God, or helping others, or something else. Spirituality has always been part of the A.A. founders' core message and approach. Now science is catching up. But what exactly is spirituality doing?

In a recent 2026 JAMA Psychiatry meta-analysis, Howard Koh and colleagues examined 55 longitudinal studies involving 540,712 people. Religious or spiritual involvement was associated with a 13% lower relative risk of harmful alcohol or other substance use. More-than-weekly religious-service attendance was associated with an 18% lower risk.

Association is not causation, but these are still impressive numbers. People involved in religious communities may also have more supportive families, different friends, greater supervision, and social expectations discouraging drug use, which may influence the numbers.

There’s another important thing to remember about this study. About 87% of the study’s extracted effects concerned prevention. Preventing addiction and treating established addiction aren’t the same thing.

Another study added important information. Paul McClure and Lindsay Wilkinson examined 1,711 adults in the Midlife Development in the United States study. People who attended substance-use recovery groups were 2-3 times more likely to identify as spiritual but not religious. More frequent participation was particularly associated with this identity.

Anyone who has treated SUDs has seen patients who seemed absolutely hopeless. But people surprise themselves and us all the time. They change in ways that cannot be explained by a negative urine drug screen.

Addiction changes priorities. Family, work, relationships, and ordinary pleasures lose their appeal. Behavior and motivation shift from everyday rewards to drugs and drug-related cues.

Drug users remember that drugs produced pleasure. But that becomes a memory. Over time, continued use becomes increasingly prompted by the need to avoid withdrawal, dysphoria, and distress. The next drink, dose, or high takes priority.

Many patients entering treatment are depressed, anxious, and unable to experience pleasure. Some have independent psychiatric disorders. Others have symptoms produced or amplified by chronic substance use and withdrawal.

Detox or cold turkey stopping the drug does not immediately restore normal brain or reward function. This is one reason early recovery is so difficult. The drug is gone, but pleasure, motivation, and hope may not have returned.

We don’t have evidence that prayer restores dopamine neurons or reverses addiction-related neuroadaptations. Those claims would go well beyond the science. But consider what happens in a recovery community. A meeting provides structure. A sponsor provides accountability. A recovering person helps someone newly sober, consolidating their own sobriety. Friendships develop. People resume positive activities they had ended with addiction.

People with SUDs find it hard to believe that helping another person can become more rewarding than getting high. But when they change, helping others can become a reason for living. These changes may be essential to sustained recovery.

The brain learns from experience. Recovery requires new experiences, new habits, and new rewards.

A.A. has been helping people recover since 1935 through personal testimony rather than rigorous clinical research. Then a 2020 Cochrane review of 27 studies found that manualized A.A. and Twelve-Step Facilitation often produced better continuous abstinence outcomes in alcohol use disorder than other established treatments.

John Kelly is the expert on how A.A. works. Kelly says that when social networks change for the better, coping improves. Abstinence becomes more acceptable, and recovery becomes part of a person’s identity. A.A. does not work because someone is told to believe in God (which A.A. does not do). It may work because people change their behavior, their friends, their expectations, and their lives.

Research is finally asking the big questions. Do religious or spiritual involvement reduce the risk of developing harmful substance use? The 2026 meta-analysis suggests it may.

Can A.A. improve recovery after alcohol use disorder has developed? Randomized trials and systematic reviews support that conclusion.

While these are different questions, we know that spirituality is relevant to SUD risk and is also very helpful in SUD treatment.

SUDs develop quickly because of secrecy, stigma, fear, and deep shame. Admitting powerlessness and ceding control to a "Higher Power"—whether defined as God, nature, or the collective wisdom of the group—can help by relieving the crushing burden of trying to control everything alone.

It is up to the individual to figure out. But some patients derive strength from organized religion. Others reject religion but find purpose in service, meditation, nature, family, or secular recovery groups.

What matters most isn’t whether someone attends church. It is whether they have relationships, purpose, and support that help them stay well.

Ask whether religion or spirituality matters to this patient. Has it helped during difficult times? Does the patient want spirituality included in treatment?

Spirituality is not a replacement for medicine, and a sponsor is not a substitute for a physician. Patients with opioid use disorder need medications like buprenorphine or methadone. Severe alcohol withdrawal requires medical detox and naltrexone. Depression, psychosis, and trauma require appropriate assessment and treatment.

Addiction hijacks the brain’s dopamine and pleasure pathways. Spiritual practices like prayer, meditation, and intense fellowship stimulate similar reward and emotional-regulation centers in the brain, affording a healthy psychological substitute. But recovery programs also change how people live, whom they trust, what they value, and what they look forward to.

Stopping drug use is essential, but so is building a life worth staying sober for.

#4809. Hyundai’s electric SUV finds some footing, with IONIQ 5 sales topping 33,000 in 2026

The Hyundai IONIQ 5 remains one of America’s most popular EVs outside Tesla, with October sales up 21%.

While the Tesla Model Y and Model 3 still dominate the US electric vehicle market, accounting for about 50% of all sales through the third quarter, it was the Hyundai IONIQ 5 that ranked third.

The market has slowed since the $7,500 federal tax credit was removed last September, with several automakers reporting fewer EV sales than in 2025 when buyers rushed to claim the credit.

Hyundai responded by cutting prices on the 2026 IONIQ 5 by up to nearly $10,000 on some trims, with a new starting MSRP of around $35,000.

As the market shows signs of recovery, IONIQ 5 sales bounced back in October, rising 21% to 1,981 units.

Through the first 10 months of 2026, Hyundai sold 33,093 IONIQ 5s in the US, still down 23% from the more than 42,700 it sold during the same period last year, when credit was still available.

Hyundai said the IONIQ 5 helped drive growth as the company posted its best October in the US ever with 73,452 vehicles sold, a 5% increase YOY.

While Hyundai sold only 169 IONIQ 9s last month (-47%), sales are still up 49% through October, with nearly 6,700 units sold.

Hyundai’s hybrids set a new October sales record, rising 20% from last year and accounting for 29% of total sales in October. Through October, Hyundai’s total US sales are up 3% YOY at 770,916 units.

Since not all automakers report monthly sales figures, it’s hard to determine where the IONIQ 5 stands through October.

Earlier today, Hyundai’s sister brand Kia reported that sales of its three-row electric SUV, the EV9, were up 11% year over year in October. EV9 sales are now up 5% year-to-date, with 13,835 units sold through October.

The cheapest 2027 Hyundai IONIQ 5 SE Standard Range starts at $35,250 and offers up to 245 miles of range.

If you want more range, upgrading to the extended-range SE RWD model costs an extra $2,500, but you get up to 318 miles of range on a single charge.

As a dietitian, I don’t hand out supplement recommendations like candy. But when it comes to products that work, creatine is one I confidently stand behind, personally use, and recommend to just about anyone. It’s one of the most well-researched, widely used, and reliable performance enhancers for boosting strength, muscular endurance, and mood, according to a 2021 study by Nutrients.

Creatine supports your body’s production of adenosine triphosphate (ATP), the fast-acting energy your muscles depend on during high-intensity effort. While you can get small amounts from food, supplementing is the most effective way to saturate your muscles. Whether you’re training consistently, getting older, or simply looking to preserve lean muscle, creatine can also speed up recovery.

To find the best creatine supplements, I tested a range of products—flavored and unflavored, pure powders, and more complex blends—paying close attention to mixability, how I felt during workouts, and any shifts in energy, strength, or recovery. Every batch is rigorously tested for contaminants and banned substances, which is especially important for competitive athletes, but just as reassuring for anyone who values transparency and quality in their supplements. Plus, it’s free of gluten, soy, and dairy. If you want a creatine that’s consistent and easy to work into your daily routine, it’s an excellent choice.Read more: Best Supplements

Each serving of two capsules provides two and a half grams of pure creatine monohydrate, so you'll need four per day to hit the research-backed five-gram dose. One quick note: They contain gelatin, so they're not suitable for vegans.

If you're still on board, these capsules deliver consistency and convenience. They're also banned-substance tested, which adds a layer of trust for athletes and anyone serious about ingredient safety.

If you travel often, mix your supplements on the go, or just don’t want to dig around for a scoop every day, Promix Non-GMO Creatine single-serve packets make things refreshingly simple. Bare Performance Nutrition (BPN) has garnered a cult-like following of fitness enthusiasts and influencers—and the efficacy and quality of their creatine proves it’s for good reason. The product is sourced from Creapure, a highly purified form of creatine monohydrate, according to Michael Hamlin, CSCS, a certified strength and conditioning specialist and the founder of Everflex Fitness. Thanks to its purity, this unflavored powder is third-party approved by Informed Sport, making it especially perfect for the everyday exerciser working on strength, power, and performance training. E

“I can actually feel and see when I’ve been taking this powder consistently,” says WH wellness writer Gabrielle Kassel. “My shoulders become more defined, my legs look stronger in my leggings, and I don’t tap out as quickly during high volume squats.” Each container also provides 60 servings, giving you a bang for your buck.

Attention competitors, Klean Athlete Klean Creatine is the best pick for you, says Lexi Moriarity, RDN, a certified sports dietitian and founder of Fueled + Balanced Nutrition. As it turns out, the product name isn’t false marketing—the powder is genuinely pure enough that it earned an NSF Certified for Sport sticker, she says. Each five-gram scoop of this supplement contains no additional ingredients but creatine. There are no artificial colors, flavorings, sweeteners, GMOs, gluten, or other mystery ingredients, which is important if you ever want to participate in a sports competition that performs drug testing.

The powder is also unflavored and dissolves easily, making it perfect for mixing into water for mid-workout hydration or adding to your pre- or post-shake.

Supplements are unregulated by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA)—and that includes creatine. As such, experts say it’s important to consider the following factors and complete your due diligence to find a high-quality product when shopping for a creatine supp. (Reading this article counts!)

Simplicity is often best with creatine. Look for products that list creatine as the sole active ingredient, ideally without added sugars, unless you're choosing a flavored version intentionally. Avoid proprietary blends that don’t disclose exact creatine content per serving.

The recommended daily dose of creatine is a minimum of five grams per day, according to the International Society of Sports Nutrition. This amount is shown to be safe and effective for maintaining creatine saturation within the muscles.

There are several types of creatine available, including monohydrate, citrate, and nitrate, but creatine monohydrate remains the most reliable. It’s the most extensively researched, dependable, effective, and cost-efficient option.

The U.S. supplement industry is largely unregulated, which means that the FDA doesn’t verify supplement marketing claims before products hit the shelves. But third-party testing can help. Look for certifications from organizations like Informed Choice or NSF Certified for Sport, which ensure the product has been tested for purity, potency, and contaminants. This is especially critical for competitive athletes concerned about banned substances.

For most people, taking creatine daily is not only okay, but it’s actually recommended to maintain optimal muscle creatine levels. Consistent daily use supports better performance, recovery, and long-term benefits.

The most common side effect of creatine is short-term water retention, which can lead to temporary weight gain. Taking more than 10 grams at once may also cause digestive issues such as bloating or diarrhea. However, for most people, creatine is well-tolerated when used as directed.

If you have pre-existing kidney or liver conditions, are pregnant or breastfeeding, or are a child or adolescent, it’s important to consult your healthcare provider before taking creatine. For most healthy adults, creatine is safe and effective, but checking in with your doctor can provide added peace of mind and guidance.

Our top picks include doormats we’ve tested in our own homes as well as a few exciting options from brands we trust, so we don’t suggest (figuratively) dragging your feet on these great designs.

Ruggable’s entire door mat catalog is machine washable, which feels like a non-negotiable for an item literally made to trap dirt. Senior commerce editor Nashia Baker found a kindred match in this pick, telling us that “the balance of whimsical lines and shapes makes walking through the door a harmonious experience.” She also noted that it’s “incredibly durable,” and after months of high-traffic it “can handle any wet or muddy shoes that land on it without getting waterlogged.” Non-slip backing keeps it (and you) from sliding around.

Lean into a modern nautical vibe (think: this contemporary Long Island escape) with Serena & Lily’s chunky mat that looks like it was woven from stolen sailboat rope. The natural/coastal blue colorway offers just a hint of color, while monochromatic options that weave in multiple shades of blue and white make a more vibrant statement.

Sometimes all you need to make a statement is a simple pattern. This honeycomb design is subtle, mildew-resistant, shed-free, and fade-safe. A rubber backing means there won’t be any slipping and it’s designed to hold water—the raised border design helps contain up to 1.5 gallons of water per square yard.

Quilt-like lines feed into a larger geometric pattern in this doormat design that still feels simple but very modern. The grid of black rectangular lines reads as a neutral, and the elongated shape covers more area than some of its peers on this list, so we’d recommend it for an entry hallway or wider doorsteps.

This Heymat doormat is a durable option for covered porches and entryways. Not suitable for true outdoor use (on an uncovered patio or anywhere susceptible to the elements), this Heymat doormat is highly absorbent and soft underfoot. Shopping market editor Kate McGregor’s family owns a few mats from this brand, which they use as an oversized entryway mat in the mudroom for muddy boots and dog paws, as well as a bathmat in the guest bathroom. “This multi-colored mat has held up so well against summer mud and dropped birdseed, despite its pastel grid design,” she says. “Even after five years, the colors have stayed vibrant, and the mat never gets soggy.” Plus, whether sprayed down or shaken, she notes that the cleanup is very easy. “I might protest if my mom ever decides to replace it.”

A departure from the traditional rectangular doormat shape, this Toast alternative offers colorful texture in one compact oval shape that’s fully reversible. This one is crafted from woven and braided jute strands that are ideal for trapping loose dirt and debris. For those looking for an alternative to standard brown jute styles, these alternating patterns are pretty mesmerizing.

If you’ve got more floor space to fill in your greeting room, smaller sizes of The Citizenry’s jute rugs could be exactly what you’ve been looking for. At 24” x 36,” this hand braided mat has a refined look thanks to the contrasting border design, and it’ll be a nice surface to station wet or damp shoes so you’re not damaging the floor.

In our doormat quest, we also found this woven gem from Matilda Goad’s MG&Co. with looped fringing that looks like scalloped edges. The deep burgundy tone will help hide visible mud stains (though the jute weave can also be easily hosed down when it’s time for a clean). It’s also available in a longer, thinner silhouette to help cover sprawling patios.

Floral without feeling overly whimsical (no shame if that’s your vibe, though), Anthropologie’s sweet, embossed doormat is a simple option for anyone with an already-decorated entryway. With an abundance of five-star ratings, lots of reviews praise the design's versatile look and durable material makeup.

The raised, slatted design of Crate & Barrel’s unfinished teakwood doormat keeps moisture, grime, and dirt away sans-bristles. It’s also great for indoor use, perhaps as a minimalist bath mat. Be mindful that teak patinas over time due to weather and regular wear and tear, shifting from a golden wood to a grayish color.

The bold tulip motif on this doormat has a cheerful Scandi-folk style that can brighten your front entry even in the dead of winter. When it starts to look a little worse for wear, the mat easily lifts off its non-slip base for machine washing. In a spot that receives near-constant foot traffic, the ability to refresh it from season to season will be a godsend.

Danish brand HAY is known for their lively color combinations, and their doormats are no exception. With interlocking strands of navy and pink rope, bookended by charming red trim, this pick welcomes guests in with a jolt of maximalist energy. The vegetable fiber strands offer a strong and durable natural alternative to plastic: Shake it out and spray it down with water to clean it and keep the colors fresh.

A stylish coir braid gives this under-$30 doormat a higher-end look. The thick weave creates an almost padded texture, designed to expertly track dirt as your shoe treads catch on the material. With its lattice-like appearance, we envision this doormat at the front door of your Cotswolds-inspired farmhouse, or perhaps a coastal home that could use another natural texture to contrast the white and blue color palette.

Leave it to Sarah Sherman Samuel to create a great doormat. The AD100 designer, arguably most known for Mandy Moore’s Altadena home, offers a twist on the traditional rectangle. Uneven stripes with cutouts give your entryway a modern edge. The coir is dependable, and the black accents help to disguise the inevitable mess.

CB2’s doormat selection is predominantly composed of versatile Chilewich designs—like this monochromatic pattern that feels like a fashionable take on television static. Designed with functionality first, the shag mat uses antimicrobial yarn to keep itself tidy. It also has a no-slip backing to keep it fixed near your doorstep, even when your shoes need a serious wipe down.

What should you look for in the best outdoor doormats?

Although design is important, you also want to make sure that your doormat is low profile enough to fit under your door and also has a non-slip backing to keep your guests from busting it before they make it into your home. (Talk about a first impression!) Materials like PVC with rubber backing are key for the latter, while 100% coir doormats give your entryway a more natural look and are more ideal for trapping dirt and debris.

The answer is a tentative yes. You’re always going to want to see what the manufacturer recommends and it, of course, depends on where you live. Doormats are always made for outdoor use, but various climates will wear down the materials differently. Frequent rain and snow might soften jute while constant sunshine will fade most textiles. An easy solution, if you aren’t sure what your mat can withstand, is to drag your doormat into the mudroom or somewhere with a bit of shelter whenever there’s big weather on its way.

#4806. Pennsylvania is way ahead on NEVI charging – now comes another $37M

Pennsylvania is putting $37 million in federal NEVI funding toward what PennDOT says will be 515 new public EV charging ports across the Philadelphia region, including curbside chargers.

The awards cover Bucks, Chester, Delaware, Montgomery, and Philadelphia counties. PennDOT says the projects will expand public charging availability by 27% across the region and 53% in Philadelphia.

For drivers without a driveway, curbside charging gives them somewhere to plug in while parked near home.

It’s Electric PA received $2.93 million for 157 on-street Level 2 ports across 13 Philadelphia neighborhoods. Voltpost received funding for another 62 curbside ports across the four suburban counties.

Fast charging is getting funding, too. PositivEnergy received $7.2 million for 54 DC fast-charging ports at 11 Philadelphia Parking Authority lots. Tesla received two $392,000 awards for eight ports each at Royal Farms in Broomall and Wawa in Plymouth Meeting.

The money comes from the federal National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure (NEVI) program, created by the Biden administration’s Bipartisan Infrastructure Law. Pennsylvania’s five-year allocation is $171.5 million.

NEVI initially focused on fast charging along designated highway corridors. States can spend the money more broadly after the Federal Highway Administration certifies that their corridor charging requirements have been met. Pennsylvania received that certification on September 22, 2025.

In fact, Pennsylvania has built 54 EV charging stations using NEVI funds so far – more than double the number of any other state.

PennDOT’s community charging program supports both Level 2 and DC fast charging. Its published program minimum requirements include at least four ports per proposed station, at least 6 kW per port, two ADA-compliant parking spaces, and J1772 or CCS connectors on every port. Equipment must also meet Buy America requirements.

PennDOT lists 71 awards in this southeastern round as part of its roughly $100 million statewide community charging effort.

Applications for the western region close November 20. Central and eastern Pennsylvania applications close March 12, 2027.

thanks for posting. PA continues to lead the country in turning this program into actual chargers. The statewide coverage is night and day from just 2-3 years ago.

For the southeastern projects, PennDOT’s estimated schedule puts environmental reviews in November 2026 through January 2027, followed by agreement execution in January and February. Drivers will still have to wait for construction and commissioning before these awards become places to plug in.

#4805. Want Studio-Style Pilates at Home? Start With These Editor-Tested Reformers

Our top picks for every kind of at-home Pilates setup, from compact machines to studio-worthy reformers.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

If you’re a pilates princess, you already know what a reformer is, and you’re well acquainted with the many ways it delivers a low-impact, strength-building workout. However, if you’re a newbie, here’s a quick crash course: A reformer is a specially designed machine, originally developed by Joseph Pilates, that consists of springs for resistance, a moving carriage, a foot bar that you push or pull, and pulleys to hold onto or hook to your feet when performing pilates exercises.

“I’d describe the reformer as a machine designed to help create an understanding of your body with resistance,” says Sam Miles, owner and co-founder of Good Time Pilates in New York City. “It gives real time feedback so you can find sensation through the shortening and lengthening of your muscles. In short and easy terms: an assist to finding your muscle engagement!”

There are unique benefits to using a reformer that are hard to replicate in a pilates mat workout, or really any other type of workout. But that doesn’t mean you have to be advanced to start using one. “The modifications to increase or decrease challenge make it a truly universal machine for any body and any fitness level, which is very unique and just awesome,” Miles says. “You can rehabilitate with a reformer, strengthen muscles, stretch and find release work, it’s the best!”

Pilates reformers are available in different types: classical and contemporary. The classical reformer stays true to Joseph Pilates’ original design; the machines are made of wood, and have springs that all have the exact same resistance level. Purists are going to want to consider these machines.

Contemporary reformers are an evolutionary riff on the original and often incorporate springs of varying resistance that can be adjusted. The dimensions also usually vary a bit from the OG classical reformer design.

While it used to be that reformers were only found in Pilates studios, more and more women are investing in a reformer as an addition to their home gym setup. There are also less intense reformer models on the market that are specifically designed for at-home use, and these generally come in at a fraction of the cost of a classical or studio-grade contemporary reformer.

After testing a bunch of options, we narrowed down our picks to a variety of machines, including commercial-grade reformers and pared-down, reimagined reformers that are made specifically to take up less space and be more affordable.

After testing a handful of Pilates reformers, the contemporary-style Balanced Body Allegro 2 came out on top for its studio-quality, strong springs, durable build, and versatile foot bar. WH fitness contributor Talene Appleton has been using it two to three times a week to practice at home for almost two years, and it’s still in mint condition. Appleton says it’s built like a tank and is commercial-grade, so it’s the best you can get for your at-home gym setup.

Five springs are featured for varying tension to accommodate different levels—three high resistance (red), one medium resistance (blue), and one light resistance (yellow), while the steel, grippy foot bar glides effortlessly for 10 vertical and horizontal positions. “I was blown away by how much the additional positions of its foot bar allowed me to change up my usual Pilates sequences,” says Appleton. “This adds incredible versatility in terms of movement options that most competitors can’t beat.” While the foot bar is its best feature, Appleton notes it’s the most difficult to set up and requires two people to line it up evenly on each side.Appleton says this machine is best for advanced users, given there’s a bit of a learning curve at first. “Using a traditional reformer at home can be a bit overwhelming at first, especially if you’re used to having an instructor call the shots in terms of spring resistance, foot bar positions, moves, and all the rest,” she says. “I found myself second-guessing my setup and wondering if I was getting the most out of each exercise (or sometimes if the move I was doing was even a real exercise at all).” She credits YouTube and TikTok tutorials for guiding her along, specifically from Balanced Body and East River Pilates.While this is the best Pilates machine money can buy (with a steep price tag of $4,345 *sigh*) it’s heavy at 157 pounds. It’s also large, at eight feet long and three feet wide, so make sure you have adequate space before splurging. It’s also not the easiest to set up. “Setting this thing up was no joke—I knew I was in for a challenge when I saw the multiple massive, heavy boxes it arrived in,” Appleton says. She notes it took her and a friend two hours to assemble.

Read More: Balanced Body Allegro 2 Review

The classical Merrithew At Home SPX Reformer is next-level if you want to up your Pilates game. It features a foldable vertical tower, which can improve flexibility and target different muscle groups with more controlled movements, adding more challenge. It has five springs—four full-resistance and one with half-resistance. Given the springs mostly have the same resistance, this machine is designed for more advanced users.

The foot bar is adjustable with four positions for different heights, while the carriage is padded for comfort. Another call-out is the included reformer box, which adds height and range of motion to moves in the seated and lying position. It’s especially helpful for those with muscle tightness or who need to modify moves involving the knees.

While this is a great reformer to elevate your practice, it’s quite large at 96 inches long and 26 inches wide. It’s also heavy at 115 pounds. Like the AeroPilates Pro XP 557, this isn’t ideal for apartments. The tower structure also requires more vertical space, so if you don’t have high ceilings, our best overall is most likely your best bet.

Read More: Best Compact Home Gym Equipment

Pretty much all pilates reformers in this guide are relatively large, but the contemporary AeroPilates Reformer 4420 is foldable. If you’re an apartment dweller, this machine is your compact answer to your Pilates reformer dreams. It can be stashed under a couch, bed, or behind a door. At 69 pounds, it’s not the lightest, so having two people for setup is probably your best bet.

Like the AeroPilates Reformer 287, it uses cords, not springs, yet delivers impressive effectiveness. This model has four adjustable cords with varying resistances and color codes, unlike the 287: two standard resistances (black), one extra intensity (red), and one light resistance (yellow). So, this reformer is good for both beginners and those who are more advanced.

It also has a built-in cardio rebounder, which is essentially a mini trampoline at the foot bar, making it an especially good choice for someone looking for low-impact cardio options and variety.

The contemporary Your Reformer is studio-grade like our best overall reformer pick, and is super durable despite being a little over half the price. During a stay in Los Angeles, Appleton rented one for at-home workouts and was extremely impressed with its easily changeable five thick springs, and a carriage that glides smoothly and quietly. The springs are also color-coded: two heavy resistance (red), two medium resistance (blue), and one light resistance (yellow).

In terms of quality, it’s a direct competitor to the Allegro 2. “The straps are thick and definitely won’t fray on me, and the strap handles are comfortable to grip, even when my palms get sweaty,” Appleton says. It’s not compact enough for most apartments, but it’s slimmer to accommodate home spaces better.

Appleton is 5’5” and found the carriage to be wide and spacious, with plenty of room to move around from supine to standing to kneeling positions. It also accommodates her much taller boyfriend, who’s “20 times more passionate about a good reformer workout,” so it’s the real deal.

The AeroPilates Reformer 287 is the most affordable option we’ve come across. It’s dramatically less expensive than our best overall—it costs under $400! But that doesn’t mean it’s less effective. Its quality is still impressive, just not studio-grade. WH entertainment editor Amy Wilkinson, an avid Pilates practitioner, was surprised by how sturdy this machine is because of its bargain price, and since it comes pre-assembled (another plus).

But, she stresses it’s best for beginners since it only features three resistance cords. “I could see someone eventually progressing beyond the capabilities of this model, especially when it comes to exercises like footwork and running, which are classically done on four springs,” says Wilkinson. “It also lacks certain accessories you’d typically find with a studio machine—a box, which is typically used for exercises in the short-box series and in a long position for pulling straps and T-press, among others.”

Speaking of resistance, unlike our best overall, this reformer uses cords instead of springs. While they can be trickier to hook on and off, their weight is identical to springs Wilkinson uses on studio-grade models.The carriage glides smoothly, although Wilkinson notes the attached handles would fall and get in the way. She recommends tossing them aside instead of hanging on the built-in shoulder blocks. As for the foot bar, it’s stable but can’t be adjusted for specific exercises.Aside from mechanics, this reformer is extremely compact, weighing just 56 pounds, and measuring 42 inches when folded and 85 inches fully extended. Wilkinson lives in a one-bedroom Brooklyn apartment and has no issues stashing it away, although she finds it tricky to fold and wide when the foot bar is attached.AeroPilates says this product can fit people up to 6'4", but Wilkinson, who is 5’11”, says even her height was pushing the machine’s limits. “I imagine anyone much taller than I am would feel a bit crunched,” she says. She also says it’s narrow, and didn’t have additional breathing room.

While most full-sized pilates reformers don’t have a built-in trampoline at the foot bar, the contemporary AeroPilates Pro XP 557 is the first full-sized model we’ve seen with a rebounder, so cardio moves like single-leg pushups and slow squats can be added to the routine. This is especially useful for beginners getting into the groove. WH associate visual editor Berkeley Brooks found it stayed sturdy when executing explosive movements at fast paces, while the material of the main carriage prevented her from slipping around.

Brooks notes that the four strong springs are easily interchangeable and have varying resistances labeled by color: two low resistance (blue) and two high resistance (yellow). The foot bar is adjustable, thick, and quiet for added comfort, and can be placed in three positions to accommodate different heights without disrupting your range of motion.

The platform is also wide at 23 inches and long at 100 inches, so this model isn’t ideal for small apartments, especially since you need additional space to execute exercises.

On the upside, Brooks says it’s easy to build and aesthetically pleasing. “I love the addition of wood to the machine because it looks great in a home gym,” she adds.

The springs in a pilates reformer are an important consideration when you’re choosing your machine. “Springs provide resistance and feedback, so the type and responsiveness of springs deeply influence your experience,” says Mo Wolfe, owner and Pilates instructor of Evolution Pilates in Port Washington, New York.

The weight of springs can also depend on whether a machine is classical or contemporary. Classical style reformers have a heavier spring tension that is the same throughout, while modern models generally tend to offer springs with a variety of resistance levels. A reformer with springs is the type you’ll find in a Pilates studio.

Alternatively, resistance cords are sometimes used in the place of springs in reformer machines that are designed for personal and at-home use. They offer similar effectiveness and are more affordable.

Taking the size of your home into consideration is important before purchasing a Pilates machine. Not only do you want to make sure you have enough room for the machine itself, you also want to make sure there will be enough space to perform the full range of Pilates reformer exercises, like leg circles, that require room to move.

Some reformers are very big and bulky, such as our pro-level, best overall selection. They take up considerable real estate and they’re best for a home gym where they can become a more permanent fixture that won’t need to be moved once it’s installed.

If your workout space is multi-functional (i.e., it’s your living room) and your equipment needs to have a smaller footprint and be more portable so you can move it around or stash it away, look for a lighter, foldable option. Just make sure that you’ll have enough space to do the moves when it’s all set up.

Since reformer Pilates is a low-impact activity, and the resistance can be so fine-tuned for your fitness level, there are no hard and fast rules about how often you do a reformer session each week. Miles says it really comes down to how your body feels. “With the variety you can get from a reformer, daily use is manageable. At my studio we have challenging classes, stretch and release classes, technique-focused classes; variety is important!” She notes that most of her clients do three reformer sessions per week.

We picked the brains of Pilates instructors to understand what to look for when shopping for a reformer, then researched dozens of the top-rated models. From there, Women’s Health writers and editors (including fitness contributors Nicolette Accardi and Talene Appleton, and entertainment editor Amy Wilkinson) tested some of the best themselves to narrow down the options.

During testing, they paid close attention to spring and cord resistance level as a measure of whether or not the machines were ideal for beginners or more advanced users. The testers also considered size, durability, and ease of assembly to determine what sorts of spaces were needed for these machiness. Moves like planks, triceps presses, running (pushing off the foot bar), chest expansions, and leg circles were all completed during our testing Pilates workouts to really put these machine to the test.

*Additional reporting by Nicolette Accardi.

#4804. The Tyranny of Romantic Possibilities

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 14, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan

James Gibson's influential notion of perceptual affordances refers to the meaningful possibilities for action that the environment offers us. A chair affords sitting, a path affords walking, and a door affords entry. I suggest that this concept can also illuminate the romantic realm. Just as the physical environment presents opportunities for action, the romantic environment presents opportunities for attachment, intimacy, desire, and betrayal. Understanding romantic affordances can help us better understand modern love.

At the heart of Gibson's ecological approach (1979) is the claim that we directly perceive possibilities for action rather than constructing them through complex inferences. Affordances are neither purely objective nor purely subjective; they emerge from the relationship between a person and the environment. Importantly, they do not disappear simply because we fail to notice them. A chair still affords sitting even when no one is sitting on it. Affordances are enduring possibilities waiting to be realized.

This perspective also highlights human freedom. Affordances offer possibilities, not necessities. They present opportunities, while leaving us free to decide which ones to pursue (Ben-Ze'ev, 1981).

"When your heart is on fire, you must realize, smoke gets in your eyes." —The Platters

The romantic environment is rich in affordances. A smile may afford intimacy. A glance may afford hope. An attractive stranger may afford the possibility of a new relationship. While Gibson's affordances involve possibilities for action, romantic affordances also involve possibilities for emotional and relational engagement.

A possibility is not the same as a reality. We are often attracted not to who a person is, but to what they might become in our lives. Sometimes we fall in love with a future rather than with a person. Unlike physical affordances, romantic affordances are notoriously ambiguous. We usually know whether a chair can support our weight. We rarely know whether another person's affection is genuine, fleeting, or merely imagined. Yet this uncertainty is often precisely what makes romantic possibilities so seductive.

Consider the familiar strategy of playing hard to get. By appearing simultaneously available and unavailable, interested and uninterested, people create competing affordances. A related assumption is that "whoever makes the first move loses." In both cases, people hesitate to appear overly eager. Ambiguity heightens desire because the outcome remains uncertain.

People are naturally drawn to what remains unresolved. The incomplete, uncertain, and partly unattainable often generates more emotional intensity than what is secure and stable. Romantic ambivalence thrives on such uncertainty. Robert Greene's (2001) portrait of the master seducer rests on this principle. Mixed signals, delayed gratification, and partial fulfillment keep multiple romantic possibilities alive at once. The attraction often lies less in what has been achieved than in what still seems possible (Ben-Ze'ev, 2024; and here).

"You can't hurry love, oh, you just have to wait. Love don't come easy, it's a game of give and take." —The Supremes

"My lover brings me tranquillity. Not during our lovemaking, which is so exciting, but as an enduring sense of inner peace." —A married woman

Modern life has dramatically expanded the number of romantic affordances surrounding us. Dating apps, social media, and increasing social mobility constantly expose us to potential alternatives. At first glance, this freedom seems desirable. Yet, as Barry Schwartz (2009) argued, an abundance of choice can become a burden. When attractive alternatives are always visible, satisfaction becomes harder to achieve. Instead of appreciating what is good enough, we keep searching for something better.

This abundance also fuels romantic ambivalence. The awareness of alternatives can undermine commitment to existing partners. Research suggests that attraction to attractive alternatives increases uncertainty about one's current relationship and diminishes both personal and relational well-being. The irony is striking: More romantic opportunities may generate greater excitement, but not greater happiness (Zoppolat et al., 2024).

Paradoxically, in a world overflowing with romantic possibilities, calmness and patience become increasingly valuable qualities of profound love (Ben-Ze'ev, 2019). A survey conducted across 116 countries and territories found that 72% of adults preferred a calm life to an exciting one, whereas only 16% preferred the opposite. The appeal of calmness extends far beyond romance.

When possibilities are abundant, the ability to devote oneself to a single relationship becomes especially valuable. Calmness and patience are therefore more than pleasant emotional states. They are ways of resisting the tyranny of endless alternatives. Such calmness is not passive. As Shunryu Suzuki (1970) observed, "Calmness of mind does not mean you should stop your activity. Real calmness should be found in the activity itself."

"True love is not a strong, fiery, impetuous passion. It is, on the contrary, an element calm and deep." —Ellen G. White

Modern romance confronts us with a paradox: freedom can become a burden. The more possibilities we perceive, the harder it may be to appreciate and cultivate the relationship we actually have. Romantic affordances create possibilities. Ambiguity makes them more alluring and their abundance makes commitment more difficult. Mature love requires choosing among them.

Indeed, one of the greatest challenges of contemporary love may not be finding romantic opportunities but resisting them. Never before have so many alternatives been so visible and so accessible. Yet no life, and no love, can flourish by pursuing every possibility. The deepest relationships are built not by maximizing options but by limiting them. A meaningful life and a profound love depend less on keeping doors open than on deciding which door to walk through. In modern romance, the greatest threat may not be the absence of opportunities, but the inability to stop pursuing them.

Ben-Ze’ev, A. (1981). J. J. Gibson and the ecological approach to perception. Studies in History and Philosophy of Science, 12, 107–139.

Ben-Ze’ev, A. (2019). The arc of love: How our romantic lives change over time. University of Chicago Press.

Ben-Ze’ev, A. (2024). Romantic affordances: The seductive realm of the possible. Philosophical Psychology, 37, 1762-1796.

Gibson, J. J. (1979). The ecological approach to visual perception. Houghton Mifflin.

Greene, R. (2001). The art of seduction. Penguin.

Schwartz, B. (2009). The paradox of choice. HarperCollins.

Suzuki, S. (1970). Zen mind, Beginner’s mind. New York.

Zoppolat, G., et al. (2024). It’s complicated: The good and bad of ambivalence in romantic relationships. Emotion, 24(5), 1190.
