#4792. The First Way of Not Being There: Detachment

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

The term dissociation, as we use it today, carries so much in just one word that it has become hard to understand what people are referring to when they say they are dissociating. This confusion exists not only in pop culture but also in the professional field. The term's popularity has made it a common protagonist in the lives of many people who use it to describe all sorts of sensations that scare them to the point of alarm. The literature also uses the term to name several mechanisms and a large number of manifestations. So, I'm trying to help separate them, as I have always been very interested in precision. I believe that if we want to understand ourselves and find solutions to our emotional problems, it's better to know what we are treating.

And it's not only me. Many people in the field have become active in developing better explanations and new ways to identify differences among dissociative experiences.

My last post was the first in a new series on dissociation where I described four concrete and different mechanisms that cause dissociative experiences. This post explains one of the four in detail: Detachment.

To explain detachment, let me start with an example. Lisa got a call from the hospital informing her that her father had had a stroke. She rushed to the hospital and remained calm while talking to the doctors, signing forms, calling her brother, and arranging for someone to pick up her kids. She was a little surprised by how little emotion she felt, but three days later, standing in her kitchen, she started sobbing and couldn't stop. She called me because she wanted to work on what she experienced.

Detachment is one of the main mechanisms behind dissociative experiences, and it's the one that situations like Lisa's may recruit to help deal with them. In detachment, the person remains aware of what is happening and what it means. Lisa knew the gravity of her father's situation. What the mechanism did was to manage how strongly she felt her emotions. Research suggests that the prefrontal cortex, which normally helps regulate emotion, applies the brakes harder on the emotional system, turning down the volume of the experience. That’s why Lisa was able to be present to handle the situation without becoming overwhelmed.

Just think about it. If she had to deal with what she was feeling and also with all the other tasks the situation required, she probably wouldn't have been able to concentrate or make the decisions she had to make. That's why the brain “lowers the volume” of the emotions. Our own sedatives also help. Under this type of intense stress, the brain releases natural opioids that reduce pain and blunt feelings.

Detachment shows up in different ways, depending on what the brain is turning down.

Emotional numbing. What Lisa experienced belongs here. Feeling is turned down. The person knows that something matters but can't really feel it. When people detach this way, they often say, “I know I should feel something.”

Physical numbness. This type is similar, but it's more somatic. What gets turned down are bodily sensations and pain. Soldiers and accident victims sometimes don't notice serious injuries until hours later.

Depersonalization. This is one version of detachment that scares many people because, when the volume is turned down, they feel as if the experience doesn't belong to them. Signals from inside the body, which normally tell us “this is me, this is happening to me,” seem to carry less weight. Brain studies have linked depersonalization to reduced activity in the insula, a region that processes those inner signals. People may feel like observers of their own lives: Their hands look like someone else's, their voice sounds strange, or they watch themselves from a few feet away. The process is meant to be temporary, and it's not dangerous on its own. It feels weird, but if the person doesn’t fight it or keep checking whether it’s gone, it may subside relatively quickly. It can be problematic if it becomes chronic, and fear of the experience can contribute to its persistence. What I mean is that fearing it may be one reason it keeps happening, and if it keeps happening, it can become a regular response of the system when there is a threat.

Derealization. This version of detachment works in a similar way to depersonalization, but what is turned down is the felt sense of the outside world instead of the felt sense of the self. Everything looks right, but it doesn't feel familiar or real. A person may say their own street looks like a movie set, or that there is glass between them and everything else. What's missing is the sense of reality that usually comes with what we see. Like depersonalization, it can be temporary and is not dangerous on its own. It doesn't necessarily cause harm to the system or leave consequences once it's over. If the brain doesn't recover its baseline, the person may become more sensitive, feel overwhelmed more easily, and predict that the detachment will return. That can make the mechanism more likely to recur, causing fear and maintaining the cycle of increasing sensitivity.

To address the mechanism, in all four versions, there are a couple of steps to keep in mind:

If you notice yourself going numb or feeling unreal, it may help to ask what your system is turning down, and why now. If it’s helping, stay there and give it time to find the assurance that you don’t need it anymore.

#4791. The 8 Best Winter Coats for Women of 2026, Tested and Reviewed in 10-Degree Weather

Our favorite on this list is from Canada Goose.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Looking for a winter coat that’ll actually keep you warm this year now that temps are finally starting to drop? We’ve got you covered—literally. At Women’s Health, our editors tested over 20 of this season’s most talked-about winter coats to find the ones that stand up to cold commutes, snowy climates, ski trips, and everything in between

From ultra-warm parkas to sleek puffers, these coats deliver on style, fit, comfort, and serious insulation from top brands like The North Face, lululemon, Columbia, Carhartt, and more. Our absolute favorite? The Canada Goose Shelburne Parka, which stands out for its stylish appearance and ability to keep us warm in extreme temps. To find the best winter coats for women, our style and gear-loving editors tested and evaluated best-selling options based on fit, materials, and warmth level. And, we wore them with tons of different clothes, like leggings with pockets, ski pants, and hoodies.

Looking for more? Check out our other winter clothing guides:

We’ve tested upwards of 20 warm winter coats, but this option from Canada Goose took the winning spot. Why? It’s super stylish, has a versatile fit, and, most importantly, it keeps us super warm in freezing weather.

WH contributor Jennifer Nied spends the colder months in Colorado, and while the NYC cold is definitely bone-chilling, the snow-capped mountains of Colorado are on a whole different level. And, as an avid hiker, Nied really got to put Canada Goose to the test. Her overall consensus: This jacket can withstand super-cold temps without slacking on style.

For a super warm puffer/parka style jacket, this coat is super stylish. The sleek, close-to-body silhouette and mid-thigh length are flattering without sacrificing warmth. We also love the oversized snorkel hood—named for the way it wraps snugly around the face—because it's incredibly cozy and super chic-looking. And, the color options are awesome, too—there’s more than just the black and brown if you’re like us and love a vivid pop of color in the colder months.

We also like this coat because it doesn’t make us feel like the Michelin Man (ha!), but still has ample room for layering underneath. It has a slightly snug fit, and is designed to be worn over light layers or under a bigger coat. But Nied says she could have sized down and still been comfortable, too.

What really sets this parka apart from others is the interior shoulder straps. "This little inside feature lets me easily slip my arms out of the sleeves without removing the whole jacket," she says. "It's handy for turning it into a makeshift backpack when I need to cool off on a crowded subway or in a store." With other coats, she usually ends up awkwardly carrying them in a big bundle whenever she's indoors, she says. There’s also a back vent with snap closures if you get overheated but don’t want to fully take the coat off.

Some additional features: The hood is just the right size—big enough to keep Nied’s head warm without causing a hair disaster. It has multiple closures, like buttons and zippers down the front. Nied is usually a size medium, and says this coat runs true-to-size. The sleeves come with a snug, sweater-like fabric at the end that she can pull over her hands to keep them warm, and the sleeves are also long enough to cover her arms comfortably.

As for warmth, this coat delivers. It’s super warm without even zipping it up—even in near-freezing temps and wind. Nied says it’s definitely the coat she'll wear when the temps plunge to zero for holiday festivities. That’s because the outside is made from a blend of cotton and polyester, which is durable and water-repellent. It’s also made with a 625 fill power made from responsibly sourced down, meaning this jacket keeps you comfortable in temps ranging from fourteen to negative four degrees Fahrenheit. The length, which hits at mid-thigh, also helps keep the chill out.

The only con we have for this jacket is the main pockets. They are lined with fleece that is so cozy for hands, but they have button-up closures instead of zippers, so our things don’t feel as secure.

WH lifestyle director Lindsay Geller is a dog owner, which means she's out early in the morning and late at night to get her pup some exercise. But, since the weather has dropped, she's been on the hunt for a coat she can wear at the chilliest times of the day to keep her warm all walk long. Lucky for her, she got to test this puffer from lululemon, which she says she's "obsessed" with.

This jacket is super sleek and basically covers your entire outfit with its calf-length design, so it's easy to throw it on over any outfit and call it a day. "I wouldn't wear this coat to a formal winter event like a wedding party, but I would pretty much wear it everywhere else like running errands or on a cold vacation," says Geller. "I wish I'd had this coat when I went to Norway last year—it would have been perfect for that."

Geller chose the black color, which she's happy about as it's super easy to style, and goes with pretty much everything.

Because this is one of lululemon's warmest jackets, you would think it would be too hot and bulky to run in, but Geller says that she was surprised at how easily it moved with her body during a morning run with her pup. "I'm used to long puffers feeling super bulky, but this one doesn't," she says, adding that it's still snug and insulated enough to keep her warm. Geller opted for a size medium, and she notes that it fits "just right." She told me that she's worn this coat on freezing cold winter mornings, and it feels like she's wrapped in an "insanely warm, yet still remarkably lightweight blanket" the entire time. "Safe to say, I'll be living in this coat until spring (at least)," she says.

Her main con is the zipper can be tricky to maneuver at the bottom, but once you hear it click, it works. However, she says it can get frustrating just trying to get the bottom part of the zipper to work.

"I absolutely adore my Columbia down jacket," says WH news and features editor Currie Engel. It's her go-to jacket for all her winter occasions.

"Lately, I've been rocking it everywhere—from the gym to dates and even at work," she says. That’s because it strikes a perfect style balance, with no over-the-top designs that lean too casual or too fancy—except maybe the fur-lined hood (which is removable!). And with a relaxed silhouette, it flatters the body without looking too bulky—despite the slightly longer mid-thigh length. This makes it a match for anything in her wardrobe.Engel opted for a size medium, and she notes that it fits perfectly. "I love the length because it’s not so long that it feels like a dress, but it's long enough to keep my whole body warm," she notes.Engel is a huge fan of how big the pockets are. "I was able to fit my wallet, phone, keys, and more in there with absolute ease (and no bulges!)." She adds that the outer fabric, which is made of polyester, is *super* luxurious and thick without the hefty price tag. The insulated interior is made of the brand's patented Omni-Heat Reflective lining, which reflects and retains body heat without adding bulk. Plus, the outer is made with 100 percent polyester, which is a welcome bonus because its small synthetic fibers help keep you super warm, and is water-resistant to help wick away sweat or light rain. It’s also insulated with 100% synthetic down—making it a more affordable option that still keeps you warm in cold, rainy weather.While there weren't many cons, Engel told me she wishes the hood could zip off.

This puffer goes all the way down past the knee to keep you nice and protected (and extra warm!). TBH, it’s hard to find a long puffer that’s actually flattering. Most look like they’re swallowing you up—but this one is a welcome exception. “It’s surprisingly lightweight, so it doesn’t look super big and bulky when you put it on,” says Lauture.

But don’t get it twisted: Although it’s light, it’s still incredibly warm thanks to a 700-plus fill power goose down insulation made to keep you comfortable in temperatures up to negative 48 degrees Fahrenheit! Plus, the 100% recycled polyester shell and lining are water-repellent and wind-resistant, making this coat a great option for a variety of climates.

Lauture also loves how versatile this coat is. And, it has many bells and whistles that make it even more worth it, like a detachable hood, thumb holes, fleece-lined pockets, and snap closures down both the front and sides of the coat. It also nails that minimalist, high-end look with its clean seams, matte finish, and perfectly relaxed fit. This jacket looks just as great with a pair of slim-fit jeans and loafers as it does with ski pants and boots.

One thing we ran into a lot with long coats is that they were too long for more petite people, but we found that this one hits at the calf no matter what height you are, short or tall. We do find that, in terms of puffers, we like the soft, airy texture of the Super Puff better than this option, as it’s a bit on the heavier side.

While the SuperPuff is on the pricier side, it’s well worth the investment for its durability and performance in harsh weather, says Saladino. “It’s not just a winter coat—it’s a statement piece that’s both functional and fashionable,” she says. Case in point: It comes in a variety of colors and lengths depending on your preference. Even the shorter hip-length version Saladino tested came in clutch for staying warm while on the go.

It stands out as one of the most stylish winter coats with its luxe, oversized fit and wide stitched panels that give it an edgy look. We also love the matte, nylon outer material and monochrome buttons that look super clean. It’s effortlessly chic and doesn’t skimp on function.

Warmth will not be questioned in this puffer. Saladino wore this during a brutally cold NYC afternoon and found that it kept her incredibly cozy. How? It’s filled with 700-plus fill-power premium down that provides some major insulation. The nylon outer is also water-repellent and wind-resistant, so you don’t have to panic if you get stuck in harsh conditions.

We appreciate that this coat has zippered pockets, so our belongings never fall out. Another bonus feature: It comes with a detachable hood. And we were pleasantly surprised that this coat runs true-to-size. We opted for our normal size and found that there was still room to fit a hoodie underneath.

This jacket is extremely warm with its fleece interior and 100% synthetic insulation, but it’s also one of the most durable options on this list. Its silicone-coated nylon exterior is water-repellent, so it keeps you dry if you get stuck in the rain or snow. Plus, it’s made with a wind-fighting nylon tech for extreme weather conditions, making it great for winter hikers. Although it has all these features, we found that the coat actually still feels lightweight. A bonus point is that it’s shorter than many other coats on this list, so it’s not as bulky and doesn't feel restrictive.

This coat gives total gorpcore vibes with its boxy fit and utilitarian details (like the patch logo and zip chest pocket) that feel effortlessly cool. The matte fabric and subtle branding add to the street-style edge that we find pairs well with everything from jeans to tailored trousers.

We also love that it comes with a hood, but it’s not removable, which marked it down a few points in our book. That being said, this coat is great for harsher conditions. Another pro? This coat comes equipped with plenty of pockets, including interior ones. So, when you’re out and about, you don’t have to worry about where you’re going to store your belongings.

In terms of size, we def recommend sizing down because this coat can look super bulky if it’s too big. However, we found that sizing down eliminated some of the thickness in the coat.

Many jackets on this list are water-resistant, but this option from Rains is fully waterproof. It kept our tester dry in light rain, thanks to the water-repellent finish. On top of that, we found this jacket to be breathable, lightweight, and super-durable. Even in the harsh NYC winds, we found that it protected us from the elements and kept us warm and dry.

Style contributor Rose Lauture recently went on a trip to Vermont and tested this coat while she was out there. “As soon as I walked out from the airport and felt the chilly air hit my face, I knew I made the right decision wearing this coat,” she says. The coat is equipped with 100% synthetic insulation and waterproof fabric which helped keep her super-warm and dry. “I spent a good amount of time outdoors in Vermont as we went hiking and played pickleball, and the coat held up well,” Lauture says.

As far as extra additions go, we love that this puffer has fleece pockets for extra warmth and a large, insulated drawstring hood for another layer of protection. Plus, the coat zips up past the neck all the way to the mouth to seal in heat.

It’s also super stylish. It’s not too puffy that it adds unnecessary width, but it still has that streetwear-esque puffer style. The rubberized, monochromatic (and weatherproof!) hardware also upgrades the look of the coat. Plus, it looks effortlessly cool when you only zip it halfway—the two-way zipper lets the coat fall open just enough to reveal the glossy interior lining, adding a cool contrast that feels very street style-ready.

We also appreciate that it comes in a variety of matte and shiny colors, so there are plenty of options to choose from. And, it’s super easy to take care of, too. “I was hesitant at first with the light color of the coat and how it might get dirty quickly, but the fabric is so easy to clean,” says Lauture, who used a cloth to wipe down the coat of any marks. However, you can easily throw it in the washer with cold water to clean it.

As far as fit goes, it is a bit oversized, but since it’s supposed to have more of that streetstyle look, we like its slightly larger fit. Want it to be a bit more snug? Opt for one size down.

In our opinion, a puffer jacket is a must-have for every wardrobe because it keeps you warm and pairs great with any outfit. But through our testing, we’ve learned that not all puffers are created equally—until we discovered this one from The North Face.

Despite its shorter length, it’s one of the best options on our list for braving the cold, thanks to ultra-warm 700-fill down insulation and an insulated hood that seamlessly packs into the collar. It’s also made with a durable nylon outer and lining, making this a great water-resistant and moisture-wicking option, too.

“This jacket is one of the warmest offerings from The North Face, and it’s also windproof, making it perfect for braving those chilly winter days,” says Saladino. Her fave feature? The tuckable hood. She loves how easy it is to fold into the collar when it’s not in use.

We also love the retro vibe of this winter jacket. It has a boxy, relaxed fit that’s super chic and flattering. According to Saladino, it has a timeless look that feels both classic and fresh. “The zip pockets on the outside are super practical, and the interior pocket means I can leave my handbag behind during the colder months,” says Saladino. “Overall, it’s a stylish, functional, and incredibly cozy choice for cold weather.” The entire jacket also easily stows into the right-hand pocket, so it’s super easy to pack.

Our one recommendation? Size up for a roomier fit. We found that going true-to-size left us feeling a bit too snug and unable to layer heavier clothing underneath. REI doesn't currently carry this red shade, but it has a cute berry colorway and neutral options to choose from.

Before buying a winter coat, think about where you’ll be using it. Are you living in a big city or a rural area? Does it get crazy cold or more temperate in the winter? How active are you? Once you've decided what you need, you can get into the nitty-gritty of coat shopping.

The key to a warm winter coat? Insulation. But there are two main types to consider: down and synthetic. Learning a bit about them can guide you in choosing the right coat for your lifestyle.

The bottom line: If you live in a wet environment and want to spend less money, go with synthetic insulation. If you live in a drier, colder place and are willing to splurge a bit more, opt for a coat that has down insulation.

You want to make sure your winter jacket is warm enough to last through many seasons. And, in order to do that, you want to make sure the materials your jacket is made of are super weather-resistant, especially if you’re in an area with harsh conditions and need extra warmth and protection. #4790. How One Creative Couple Found Harmony in Their 1920s Los Angeles Craftsman

Nothing about where interior designer Harrison Soll is now was part of the plan. Five years ago, he was focused on his work, and he didn’t want any distractions. But when he met Rodney Burns, a stylist and owner of the legendary Los Angeles vintage gallery, Church Boutique, it set everything on a new path. They met in the fall; by New Year’s they were a couple. “I didn’t think it was going to be a relationship,” Soll says. He credits their shared interests for bringing them together: “We always found a throughline with design.”

They now live in a 1925 craftsman house in Laurel Canyon. Soll took the lead decorating the nearly 1,400-square-foot home in a combination of his and Burns’s styles with many pieces coming from Burns’s eclectic collection of vintage art, furniture, and sculpture. Burns has worked with Lenny Kravitz as a stylist and creative collaborator for the past 15 years, and the singer says he admires what Burns and Soll have created together. “The mix of Rodney’s early- to midcentury style mixed with ethnic expression next to Harrison’s bold minimalist modern approach seamlessly blend together,” Kravitz tells AD.

The backyard of Soll’s and Burns’s Laurel Canyon home is a bricolage of funky, inherited stonework and vintage pottery.

The nail art above the fireplace has a cute backstory story: Burns and Soll had seen it at a vintage shop in Santa Monica and Burns regretted not buying it. When he went back to purchase the piece, it was marked as sold. But only because Soll had already covertly bought it as a Valentine’s Day gift for Burns.

The giant Sergio Bustamante giraffe bust in the foyer is a delicate topic. “The giraffe was one of our biggest fights in decorating this house,” Burns explains. “I was determined to have that giraffe live some place in this house because he’s just fantastic, and the scale of him, and the rarity of him.” Except, counters Soll, that the placement of the giraffe is treacherous because the front door swings right in its path. “You just have to be careful,” Soll says.

The foyer—which features a collection of masks and vintage paintings—was one of the most difficult areas to style, explains Burns. The couple was trying to be selective of what pieces to incorporate from Burns’s massive collection and at one point Burns suggested putting all of his masks in storage to save for another house down the line, or passing them onto Burns’s vintage boutique, Church. Soll dissented, saying, “No, let’s put them everywhere.”

The living room features two sofas—a Joseph D’Urso for Knoll piece reupholstered in leopard fabric and a leather De Sede Terrazza. The carpet is the Antilocarpa style from Stark. A trio of fiberglass shell art was sourced through Kelly Wearstler. The art behind the sofa is a manipulated canvas garment bag by the artist Roosevelt “Rip” Woods, the first black artist to have a solo show at the Phoenix Art Museum.

As renters, there were naturally limitations on what could be achieved. Soll got permission to retile a bathroom and install a new vanity. The doe-patterned wall-to-wall carpeting in the living room was an “ask for forgiveness” move, but his landladies ended up loving it. Burns, on the other hand, needed more convincing. “The carpet took many dinners of conversations between the two of us,” Soll says.

Soll describes himself as more of a minimalist while Burns avows, “I’m a maximalist to the umpteenth power.” The couple attempted to strike a balance while still filling the space with character. Some rooms nod to Soll’s leanings toward minimalism like an office with a midcentury desk and a 1970s tapestry and the dining room where a Sergio Bustamante table and a Chinese Art Deco rug are the main attractions.

When decorating their Laurel Canyon home, Soll and Burns had to figure out how to combine their opposing styles, with Soll being more of a minimalist and Burns being a maximalist. But, says Burns, “[Soll] has made me be able to take a pause and then also make me a little less attached to some of the things that I’ve collected  and given me an opportunity to maybe show a little bit more restraint.” In the corner, a brass Maison Jansen palm tree mingles with a Sergio Bustamante monkey.

Burns, who has been styling Lenny Kravitz for over a decade, says his approach to home design and fashion are one in the same: “Building an outfit, building a room: same thing in my opinion.”

Kravitz offers these kind words on Burns: “What I love about Rodney is that he is limitless in his concepts and always thinks outside of the box. His visual vocabulary enables him to mix a vast stew of eras and genres. He pays tribute to our ancestors and uplifts new innovators. Always soulful, expressive, and elegant.”

In the dining room, Soll placed a Sergio Bustamante table on a diagonal to make enough room for the couple’s large dog. “She’s a girthy girl,” says Soll, referring to the table, not the dog. The chairs are by Paul Evans and the Chinese Art Deco rug was sourced from Ariana Rugs. The Tom Greene chandelier was sourced from Burns’s boutique, Church.

Burns’s maximalism is on display in the living room, where a couch upholstered in leopard Scalamandré mixes with zebra-hide chairs and a sinuous De Sede sofa. (That animal print couch, Soll wants you to know, also features a block of leather upholstery: “I just think it would have been too maximalist to do a full Scalamandré sofa.”)

The living room is filled with brass sculptures (a Maison Jansen palm tree and a Sergio Bustamante monkey), bronze figures sourced from an estate sale in Arizona, and several pieces of sculptural artwork.

The bedroom mixes patterns and textures with a stainless steel bed from TTMM, Paul Evans “Cityscape” nightstands, striped bedding, and antique bronze table lamps with African mud cloth shades.

The 1970s textile art in the office is a vintage find of Burns’s that Soll loves. “I used to go to Rodney’s apartment when we first started dating, and I would be like, ‘Oh my God! Like, if we break up, I’m never gonna be able to find this tapestry,’” he says.

Soll got permission from his landladies to retile the bathroom and add a new vanity. The metal Curtis Jeré artwork comes from Burns’s collection.

The bohemian architecture of the home lends quirkiness to the design. The main bedroom isn’t a perfect square, making it seem like a stainless steel bed from TTMM is placed on a diagonal but is actually following the geometry of a very funky, angular bedroom.

The couple has taken their time tinkering and adjusting the decor, taking a considered approach to collecting and combining their belongings. Soll describes the overall vibe as having an Afrocentric theme that’s also a little bit Ralph Lauren. “Our visions have mingled,” Burns says.

Still, there is one last item the couple needs to complete the design: a blanket basket. But, says Soll, “We still haven’t found one we agree upon.”

The backyard is also home to a shed (not pictured), which functions as Burns’s closet.

#4789. Puerto Rico tapped Sunrun’s home batteries for 18 straight days

Sunrun has doubled participation in its Puerto Rico virtual power plant to more than 60,000 customers, and the grid is putting those home batteries to work: It tapped into them for 18 straight days in October.

A virtual power plant (VPP) connects batteries across thousands of properties and coordinates them to supply power together.

Sunrun says its VPP network in Puerto Rico now includes nearly 70,000 batteries, frequently delivering 45 megawatts (MW) for four hours at a time. It has dispatched them more than 60 times since April, including daily deployments beginning October 13 during unusually hot weather.

For Puerto Ricans, who pay some of the highest electricity prices in the US, getting reliable power for all that money remains a problem. Residential electricity averaged 26.36 cents per kilowatt-hour in August, compared with a US average of 18.16 cents, according to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA).

That makes the batteries already installed at homes pretty useful. The grid can pay to tap their stored energy when supplies get tight, putting existing equipment to work without waiting for a new power plant to be built.

Sunrun’s network grew from around 4,000 customers in 2024 to more than 30,000 in 2025. It says it’s the largest aggregator in Puerto Rico’s Customer Battery Energy Sharing (CBES) program.

LUMA, the island’s grid operator, calls on CBES when it expects electricity demand or reserve needs to exceed available generation. Companies such as Sunrun then manage the battery response automatically.

Homeowners get paid for sharing energy and choose how much to keep for backup. Sunrun says most share a small portion of their total battery capacity; the company earns recurring revenue for operating the network.

Across the wider CBES program, LUMA reported in July that more than 90,000 participating customers had helped provide an average of 75 MW during generation shortfalls.

Puerto Rico’s reliability problem goes well beyond hurricanes.

Customers averaged 36 hours without power in 2025, even excluding major events, according to the US EIA. That’s up 19% from 2024. Mainland US customers generally experience about two hours a year under the same measure. Major events added another 23 hours of outages on the island.

More batteries can help, but the size of the shortfall still matters. In an April regulatory filing, participating aggregators said the program couldn’t prevent every rolling blackout in 2025 because some supply gaps exceeded its roughly 50 MW of four-hour capacity. They’re looking to enroll more batteries so the program can cover larger shortfalls.

#4788. Want to Turn Back the Clock? These 10 Diets May Help You Age Better

You’ve got way more options than just the Mediterranean diet.

When healthy aging is the goal, it makes sense to try everything you can to make it happen. That means doing your best to exercise regularly, keep up with doctor's appointments, and eat a well-balanced diet. You have lots of options when it comes to the last one—but it can be hard to know which of the many popular eating plans is right for you. Thankfully, new research has helped narrow the choices.

The study, which was published in Nature Communications, analyzed several different diets to see how they impacted biological aging. (Biological aging is the age of your cells, while your chronological age is how old you are.) Popular eating plans like the Mediterranean diet and the DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) diet made the cut, of course, but several lesser-known diets did too. Here’s what to know.

Meet the experts: Jessica Cording, RD, author of The Little Book of Game-Changers; Keri Gans, RD, author of The Small Change Diet; and Sonya Angelone, RD, PhD, a former spokeswoman for the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics and a San Francisco-based dietitian.

For the study, researchers analyzed data from 6,470 participants who were 30 and older. Researchers looked at some of the participants' biomarkers that correlated with biological age and compared that with information about their diets.

After analyzing the data, researchers found that healthier eating in general was linked with slower biological aging, no matter which diet people chose. Each specific eating plan offered an edge with certain perks, though. Case in point: The DASH diet (which is specifically meant to stop hypertension) had more cardiovascular benefits for biological aging, while the MIND diet (which combines the Mediterranean and DASH diets for brain health) offered cognitive perks. But researchers discovered that there were a lot of shared biological aging benefits between the different types of diets.

These are the 10 diets flagged as being good for biological aging:

All of these diets are slightly different, but there are a few common threads. "They generally emphasize fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and other nutrient-dense foods," says Keri Gans, RD, author of The Small Change Diet.

The diets also stress the importance of minimally processed foods, while limiting refined carbs, added sugars, and processed meats, according to Sonya Angelone, RD, PhD, a former spokeswoman for the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics and a San Francisco-based dietitian. "The recommended foods provide fiber, antioxidants, polyphenols, vitamins, minerals, and healthy fats that support metabolic health and help protect cells from oxidative stress and chronic inflammation," she says. Oxidative stress and chronic inflammation are both linked to a higher risk of disease, Angelone points out.

These diets also support the heart, brain, and digestive systems, says Jessica Cording, RD, author of The Little Book of Game-Changers. "All of these things factor into the aging process and somebody's quality of life as they age," she says. "When you're eating to support these different organ systems, you support your longevity and lower your risk of disease."

There are a few things to take away from the findings, according to dietitians. One is that there isn't a single eating plan that's superior to others when it comes to longevity. "It's the overall quality of what we eat consistently that matters most, rather than following a particular diet or avoiding individual foods," Gans says.

While there are plenty of diet plans out there that claim they can help you live longer, Angelone stresses this: "Healthy aging doesn’t have to include expensive foods, supplements, or restrictive diets."

Finally, the study underscores the power of nutrition in keeping you healthy. "Our genes are not our destiny," Angelone says. "We can change the expression of our genes—genomics—with nutrition and lifestyle habits."

Supporting healthy aging with the way you eat means giving your body the fuel it requires to function well, Angelone says. "Healthy aging isn’t about finding a perfect diet or miracle food or supplement," she says. "It is about consistently providing foods that supply nutrients needed by our bodies to function optimally, repair cellular damage, and protect themselves. This will impact how we age."

#4786. 10 Ways to Find Out if Your Partner Is Lying to You

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 14, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

Partners in a romantic relationship rely on each other to be truthful. It can be both unnerving and stressful to wonder if your partner isn’t holding to this standard. Kim and Chris are in a stable long-term monogamous relationship, but lately Kim has begun to wonder if Chris means what he says. In the latest incident, an important one, Chris promised that they would take their relationship one step further toward commitment. But so far, nothing has happened. What makes this particularly odd is that Chris has seemed to be honest and authentic, not just in the relationship, but in general. Maybe it’s all been a fraud, though.

Because couples in committed relationships share so many aspects not only of their lives but of their vulnerabilities, hopes, and aspirations, it is particularly important for the relationship’s health that they don’t lie to each other. As noted in new research by the University of Copenhagen’s Rachele Mazzini and colleagues (2026), although honesty is a fundamental “relationship ‘rule,’” “dishonesty occurs regularly in romantic relationships.”

Dishonesty can take the form of telling falsehoods, but it can also show up as keeping secrets. Once the dishonesty starts, in whatever form, it can spiral out of control. But all of this begs the question of why someone would lie in the first place. After all, if you love someone, what would lead you to disguise the truth? Mazzini et al. believe that the motives behind dishonesty are as important as the behavior itself. Or, the person may just be an inveterate liar who does so for no particular reason at all.

Previous studies have examined different types of lies, motives for lying, and personality traits associated with lying, but none have addressed directly the question of how to measure lying in relationships. The U. Copenhagen team decided to address this very problem.

Mazzini and colleagues began their quest by asking preliminary samples of online participants to complete a 47-item version of what became, as tested in the final sample, a 10-item Dishonesty in Intimate Relationships Scale (DIRS). They administered the DIRS two times, one week apart, in this final sample of nearly 900 participants. This allowed them to analyze its value in predicting relationship outcomes above and beyond other measures of deception. The relationship outcomes included how well a couple was functioning in terms of trust, ambivalence, closeness, and authenticity.

Here are the 10 items on the DIRS; each should be rated from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree); an (R) indicates the item is reverse-scored:

Items 1 to 6 fall into the Deception factor and 7 to 10 into the Infidelity factor.

Based on mean scores the authors report in supplemental materials, their final online sample tended toward the honesty end of both subscales. The least likely to be endorsed was item 7, and the highest were items 2 and 3. Most items ranged between 2 and just about 2.5.

Correlation between DIRS subscales and the other relationship measures showed that all high DIRS scores bode poorly for relationship quality. Furthermore, based on the one-week separation between the two times of testing, it appeared that the DIRS also went above and beyond other deception measures in predictive value.

There were some connections between DIRS scores and personality measures of dishonesty, but this makes sense. A liar will be a liar, no matter what, which will spill over into a close relationship. As stated more formally by the authors, “domain-specific dishonesty in relational contexts is not fully separable from broader dispositions.”

So far, you may have learned about how much you tend to lie in your relationship compared to those in the online sample, but what about measuring your partner? If, like Kim, you suspect something is going on, you probably won’t want to hand this scale over to your partner and demand completion.

Instead, you can use the DIRS as an inner check as you navigate the ins and outs of your daily experiences with your partner. Do you notice that details are sometimes eliminated from stories your partner tells you? Like Kim, does it seem that your partner says things just to please you when it comes to taking your relationship to the next level? A promise-based white lie can be a true danger signal, especially when you think the lie is meant to protect your feelings.

You might also notice something off in the Infidelity domain. People in the Mazzini et al. study were unlikely to admit to cheating, and they also tended not to say they would become emotionally involved with someone else. But you may notice your partner making excessively complimentary remarks about someone else if not directly flirting at social gatherings (while ignoring you). In-jokes, winking, and more than a few "friendly" lunch dates can be another clue.

To sum up, it can be helpful to have a short measurement guide in your back pocket to check whether your partner truly has your best interests at heart. If something seems “off” from time to time, the DIRS can provide a good reality check. Relationship fulfillment requires honesty, and when it’s not there, it may be time to figure out how to get back on track.

Mazzini, R., Malfilâtre, A. L., Power, S. A., Zettler, I., & Lilleholt, L. (2026). Development and validation of the Dishonesty in Intimate Relationships Scale (DIRS). European Journal of Psychological Assessment. https://doi.org/10.1027/1015-5759/a000970

#4785. Xiaomi’s humanoid robots work a full 8-hour shift in its EV factory

Xiaomi has released footage of its humanoid robots working a full 8-hour shift at its EV factory, sorting center console side covers for its cars. The company says the robots did it on their own, catching and fixing their own mistakes along the way.

If that’s fully autonomous, it’s truly impressive. But we’ve been disappointed by humanoid robot demos before, and Xiaomi left out the numbers that would let anyone check.

Xiaomi Tech posted the video on X on November 3, as the company picked up awards at the World Internet Conference in Wuzhen. It shows the robots pulling side covers from bins, carrying them to storage racks, and placing them into slots, with a running clock of cumulative working time and an “Autonomous, 100x Speed” label in the corner.

8 hours on the production line. 🤖Xiaomi’s full-size humanoid robot takes on an 8-hour task at the Center Console Side-Cover Sorting Workstation at Xiaomi Auto Factory.Beyond sustained operation, it can autonomously detect and correct anomalies while coordinating with the… pic.twitter.com/brpO3S5bCn

According to Xiaomi, the robot covered the full day of production needs at that workstation. The company says it detected and corrected anomalies on its own and coordinated with the production line’s control system, calling it “another step toward real-world industrial deployment.”

This is the third milestone in a program Xiaomi has been running in public all year. In March, it put a humanoid in its Beijing EV factory as an “intern” installing self-tapping nuts. Xiaomi reported a 90.2% success rate over three hours, fast enough to meet the station’s 76-second cycle time. By July, it said that success rate was up to 98%, and it added two harder stations, including the side-cover sorting job from this week’s video.

Last December, Xiaomi’s CEO, Lei Jun, said the company plans to deploy humanoid robots in large numbers across its factories within five years.

Xiaomi also announced that its open-source Xiaomi-Robotics-1 AI model, pre-trained on 100,000 hours of real-world robot data, has started trial runs in Xiaomi staff apartments. In a 30-minute run, it completed more than 50 task chains across three rooms.

Xiaomi didn’t say how many parts the robots sorted, what the success rate was over eight hours, or how many times a human had to step in. It also didn’t explain how the robots stayed powered for a full shift: swapped batteries, a tether, or charging breaks.

And that matters, because “autonomous” in a robot video can mean anything. Tesla’s Optimus robots at the 2024 “We, Robot” event were remotely operated by humans, which Tesla didn’t disclose at the time. Last December, an Optimus took a suspicious tumble in a Miami demo, raising its hands to its head like a teleoperator pulling off a VR headset as it fell.

To be fair to Xiaomi, it has published success rates and cycle times for its earlier factory tests. That’s more than Tesla has ever shared about Optimus doing useful work, and Tesla now says it won’t deliver Optimus to outside customers until late 2027.

The most interesting moment in the video comes around the 1:37 mark. In a segment Xiaomi labels “Dropped Material: Multi-Robot Collaboration,” a humanoid upper body mounted on a wheeled base rolls in to help the two legged robots.

It’s not the only thing on wheels in that scene, either. The bins of parts are shuttled around by autonomous mobile robots, the same kind of wheeled platforms that have been moving materials in car factories for years.

They could have got a lot more done if they'd moved the parts bins closer so the bots didn't have to walk as far. That's a huge open space between the two.

If this demo was truly fully autonomous for eight hours, with the robots handling their own errors, that’s one of the more impressive humanoid demos we’ve seen. Xiaomi deserves credit for putting its robots on a real production line and publishing some real numbers along the way. But we’ve been burned by “autonomous” robot demos before, so we’ll wait for more details before getting too excited.

The wheeled robot is our favorite part of the video, though. It’s a great example of why you shouldn’t bet everything on the humanoid form factor. Wheels are far more efficient than legs on most terrain, and a flat factory floor is the best-case scenario for wheels. A wheeled base doesn’t burn energy just to stay upright, it’s more stable when carrying parts, it has room for a much bigger battery (which would solve that 8-hour power question), and it needs fewer expensive actuators.

The value in these robots is in the hands, arms, and the AI driving them. Legs make sense in homes with stairs, and maybe that’s where Xiaomi wants to take them eventually. But factories were designed around carts and forklifts, not people walking around carrying parts.

#4784. How to Lose Weight Naturally, According to Experts

Here are 10 easy-to-follow tips to speed up the process—and make it more enjoyable.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Starting a weight-loss journey is no easy feat. There’s a lot to think about, between getting into a regular workout routine, changing up what you eat, and maybe even considering a GLP-1 medication.

But at its core, weight loss is about developing a healthy, sustainable relationship with food and movement. You don’t have to make a dozen changes all at once—the goal is long-term success, even if it’s a slow process. That’s why you should aim to lose one to two pounds a week, says Danielle Crumble Smith, RDN, a dietitian at Eat Well, Live Well. Working out at a manageable pace, eating balanced meals, and making maintainable changes can help you feel your best.

Meet the experts: Danielle Crumble Smith, RDN, is a nutritionist at Eat Well, Live Well. Kami Blease, CPT, is a personal trainer at Fyt Personal Training. Tatyana Johnston, CPT, is a former Nike master trainer and event specialist at Lululemon. Jordan Hill, RD, is a nutritionist with Top Nutrition Coaching.

Ahead, experts share their 10 best tips to make your weight-loss journey successful.

First, be sure to consult your doctor—they’ll help you set mindful, attainable goals that will keep your body healthy and strong. Then, try implementing more of these habits into your lifestyle:

Take the stairs every day at work or hold a quick plank first thing in the morning. "All these things add up over time," says Kami Blease, CPT, a personal trainer at Fyt Personal Training. "I recommend finding things you could do almost daily.”

Additionally, try adding a brisk 30-minute walk into your day (even if it’s broken up into three 10-minute walks) to increase calorie burn and push you closer to your weight-loss goals, per the Mayo Clinic. "It's low impact and not a super strenuous form of movement, which increases the chances that someone will stick with it,” says Tatyana Johnston, CPT, a former Nike master trainer and event specialist at Lululemon. "Just remember to recover with hydration, fuel, and stretching.”

Burn fat and build muscle with the WH+ 4-week walking plan

Strength training “helps with balance and stability, improves metabolism, and even lowers your risk of certain diseases," says Blease. Resistance training has also been found to help with weight loss and body recomposition, according to a 2026 study in Frontiers in Endocrinology that had 304 adults follow a calorie-restricted diet and either resistance train, do aerobic exercise, or no exercise for 1 to 18 months.

To get comfortable with form, try practicing bodyweight exercises first, Blease recommends, then add weights after you’ve mastered the move. This can help you focus on progressive overload—which means gradually increasing the weight, frequency, or number of reps over time, Blease says. Eventually, you should aim to work all major muscle groups at least twice a week, per the new ACSM resistance training guidelines.

Cardio can also help with weight loss—the CDC recommends 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity (such as brisk walking) per week, or 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity activity (like running) each week. However, this number can vary based on someone’s individual health, and the intensity of the cardio. "Consistency is key. If you can establish and stick to a cardio schedule, you have a better chance at losing weight and keeping it off," Johnston says. Playing sports, working out with friends, or listening to a podcast during cardio can help boost your motivation too.

Also, if you enjoy high-impact exercises and want to lose weight fast, HIIT workouts can be a great way to expend a lot of energy in a short period of time. "You can ramp up the intensity by trying to get in more reps during a certain amount of time or using heavier weights while maintaining the same time goal,” says Blease. “Both will increase your intensity and continue to challenge your body."

If the gym or workout classes aren’t really your speed, choose a form of movement that you love so you can stay consistent with it. “Hiking, swimming, skiing, surfing, or biking are all forms of movement that might feel more sustainable,” says Blease.

"Start smaller than you might think," Blease says. "Often, people overcommit because they are excited. However, it's then easy to get burnt out." After a few weeks, add in a second day, and when that feels seamless, try a third, and over time, you'll find a cadence that works for you, she adds.

Just make sure you always have at least one rest day. "People can get so fixated on weight loss that they end up [overdoing exercise and] hurting themselves," Blease says. "Take time to stretch, rest, and recover as needed."

"Having a trainer create a program that is specific to your needs ensures that you are more likely to get the results you are looking for—and keep your body safe in the process," says Blease. They can help you lose fat while building muscle, which can better your overall metabolic health and insulin sensitivity, and regulate blood sugar to support a healthier body recomposition.

A trainer will also make sure you maintain proper form and that you stay consistent. Decide on a number of days per week that fits your goal and budget, and ask your trainer to help hold you accountable, Blease says.

Research suggests that working with a personal trainer may have more profound effects on weight loss: A 2024 study in Heliyon had 66 adults train individually, with a partner, or a personal trainer over 12 weeks, and they monitored their improvements in bench presses, squats, skeletal muscle mass, and fat mass. The group that worked with a personal trainer improved their leg training and reduced fat mass compared to the other groups.

Protein can help you stay full throughout the day, stabilize your blood sugar levels, and synthesize muscle mass, Smith says, helping with weight loss. While individual dietary needs vary, you can generally aim for 30 to 35 grams of protein per meal to help you stay full throughout the day. Some good sources include eggs, poultry, seafood, red meat, beans, peas, lentils, legumes, nuts, seeds, and soy, per the current Dietary Guidelines for Americans.

Additionally, "fiber is more slowly digested and helps keep you feeling full for a longer period,” Smith adds, recommending vegetables. Increased vegetable intake is also linked to lower blood sugar levels, lower triglycerides, and can help promote liver function. If you don't love veggies, you can also puree them and add them to a sauce or weight-loss-friendly smoothie.

Lastly, don’t forget about healthy (unsaturated) fats—which can help provide energy, per the Mayo Clinic. Try avocados, extra-virgin olive oil, nuts, seeds, soybeans, and seafood.

"Drinking enough water can help you to feel full and prevent overeating," says dietitian Jordan Hill, RD. Aim to drink about half your body weight in ounces of hydrating fluids per day.

Also, avoid sugary beverages. "Juices, sodas, and fancy coffees are often the calorie-equivalent of a meal, yet they will still leave you hungry," says Smith. "The sugar content is often more than a candy bar, which will cause blood sugar levels to rise." Instead, replace your beverages with fruit-infused water, herbal tea, or coffee with cinnamon or zero-calorie sweeteners.

Avoid foods that are high in added sugars, unhealthy fats, and empty calories, which can contribute to weight gain, says Hill: "Instead, focus on eating whole, nutrient-dense foods that will provide your body with the nutrients it needs."

Listening to your internal cues of hunger and fullness can help you control portion sizes, which can also aid weight loss. "Honoring fullness can help prevent overeating and ensure that you're not consuming more calories than your body needs," says Hill. Keeping a food journal can also help you become more mindful of what you're eating, when, and how you're feeling throughout the process of losing weight.

“When you skip meals or go too long in between meals or snacks, you get overly hungry. This makes it much more difficult to make healthy choices, and it also makes it harder to not overeat later," says Smith. Skipping meals can also result in a slower metabolism and leave you feeling fatigued, which can negatively impact your workouts both in effort and recovery.

If you struggle to eat consistent meals, Smith recommends munching on small snacks throughout the day. “Set yourself up for success by bringing healthy snacks with you when you’re away from home, so you’re not caught in a situation where you are really hungry but have no access to healthy food,” she says.

If you need extra assistance, a dietitian can analyze your diet and recommend personalized tips for how you can eat to lose weight, which may be more helpful than doing it on your own. A 2025 review of articles on weight-loss interventions provided by a dietitian for overweight and obese adults in the Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics looked at how working with a dietitian improved their health markers, as opposed to not working with one (the control group). The group that worked with a dietitian had improved weight loss, waist circumference, blood pressure, and quality of life compared to the control group.

When you encounter a setback (like when you skip a few days of workouts), it can be discouraging and all-consuming, and can cause you to fall off track. "One of the most crucial components of successfully reaching a goal is to not let setbacks ruin our progress,” says Johnston. “The setback is often not as severe as we think, and will not impact our end goal very much at all.”

Just take a breath and realize we’re all human and mistakes are normal; then move forward with your health plan in mind.

And don’t forget to be kind to yourself. Practicing self-compassion and returning to your plan will help reinforce your goal and remind you that this weight-loss journey requires patience and perseverance. "Practice giving yourself grace when [you] slip up,” Johnston says. “As long as it doesn’t become a habit, you will continue moving forward towards your goal.”

#4783. BYD’s new luxury electric SUV has one big problem: It weighs over 8,200 lbs

BYD’s new full-size electric SUV, the Denza N9 EV, was revealed in a regulatory filing, weighing in at over 8,200 lbs (3,760 kg). That creates one issue.

The Denza N9 first went on sale last March, a flagship plug-in hybrid (PHEV) SUV with a combined CLTC range of about 807 miles (1,300 km) on a full charge and full tank of gas.

BYD introduced the updated Flash Charging version earlier this year, which uses its second-generation Blade Batteries and delivers a pure electric CLTC range of 260 miles (420 km). Combined, it gets up to 944 miles (1,520 km) under CLTC conditions.

In the latest batch of new energy vehicles (NEVs) approved for sale by China’s MIIT (Ministry of Information Technology) this week, a new all-electric Denza N9 appeared.

The filing revealed the Denza N9 EV will be available with three electric motors, delivering a combined output of 1,193 horsepower (890 kW).

A badge on the back reveals it will use BYD’s tri-motor e3 platform. The setup features a single 362 horsepower (270 kW) front motor and two 415 horsepower (310 kW) rear electric motors.

The electric version measures 5,270 mm long, 2,030 mm wide, and 1,830 mm tall, with a 3,125 mm wheelbase, which is the same as the current Denza N9 PHEV Flash Charging model. It will be available in five- and six-seat configurations.

While the filing reveals it will use a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery with cells from BYD’s battery unit, FinDreams, it does not provide specifics like capacity or driving range.

One relatively big thing to note: the Denza N9 EV has a gross weight of 3,760 kg, or about 8,289 lbs.

Obscene weight , and that applies to other SUVs as well. Vehicle registration taxes should be based on vehicle weight as it wears out roads and endangers other road users and infrastructure and wastes resources.

As AutoNext points out, this makes it too heavy for an EU category B driving license, which covers up to 3,500 kg (7,716 lbs).

Last year, the EU updated the rules, allowing drivers who have held a category B license for two years to drive alternative-fuelled vehicles with a maximum weight of up to 4,250 kg (9,369 lbs).

While the Denza N9 EV would qualify as listed, newer drivers would still need a commercial EU category C1 driving license to drive it.

BYD launched its luxury sub-brand, Denza, in Europe and the UK in March, starting with the Z9 GT and the D9 van. More recently, it introduced the Bao 5 PHEV SUV and the Denza Z electric supercar.
