#4755. BLUETTI’s flexible $1,099 Apex 200 backs up your home – and powers your RV

What do you actually need to keep running when the power goes out? For most households, the fridge, wifi, phones, and a few other essentials come first. Buying enough battery storage for every appliance in the house can come later – and that’s the appeal of BLUETTI’s latest launch, the Apex 200 portable power station.

The Apex 200 starts with 2.56kWh of storage and 3.2kW of continuous AC output, with the option to add batteries when you need longer backup. Built-in RV connections also mean it can earn its keep between blackouts.

BLUETTI launches the Apex 200 on November 4, with standalone super early-bird pricing starting at $1,099 through November 18. Electrek readers can get an extra 5% off with code ELECTREK5OFF.

Here’s how to work out which setup is worth buying for your home or RV.

The Apex 200 takes the expandable design of BLUETTI’s flagship Apex series and puts it in a smaller package.

You get a 2,560Wh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery. The 3.2kW of continuous AC output increases to 3.6kW when an expansion battery is connected or the unit is actively charging.

The enclosure holds all that in 36.2 liters and weighs 26.9kg (59.3 lb). You’ll want two hands to move it, but it’s convenient to move it between home and your camper.

BLUETTI’s UltraCell technology delivers an industry-leading energy density of 70.7 Wh/L, yet the Apex 200 is more than 50% smaller by volume than class competitors. For an RV owner, that smaller footprint frees up room for other gear.

There’s also a tilted display and four app-controllable AC outlets. That might not sound like a big deal, but when the battery is on the floor or under your desk and you want to check or redirect its charge, it means you don’t have to crouch.

BLUETTI calls its approach “Start Small. Scale Big. Power More.” BLUETTI says Apex 300 users reported liking the modular design but wanted something easier to handle day to day. The Apex 200 offers them a lower entry point, with room to add capacity rather than replace the main unit.

Before buying a portable power station, you’ll want to know how much power your appliances draw and how much energy they use over time.

For example, a 150W appliance running continuously for 10 hours uses 1,500Wh. A 1,500W appliance gets through that same amount in one hour. Running a coffee maker briefly is a different proposition from keeping a high-draw appliance on all afternoon.

A rough runtime calculation is: Usable battery capacity in watt-hours ÷ average load in watts = hours of operation.

Divide the Apex 200’s nominal 2,560Wh by a steady 150W load, and you get about 17 hours before accounting for conversion losses and the battery system’s own power use. Real runtime will be lower.

Refrigerators complicate that calculation because their compressors cycle on and off. Check measured daily energy use where possible, along with startup demand – motors can briefly draw more power when they kick on.

If your usual blackout lasts four to 12 hours, start by looking at the Apex 200 on its own.

BLUETTI estimates it can run a 150W refrigerator for 10–12 hours, or support low-draw essentials such as CPAPs, wifi routers, and mobile devices for two to three days, depending on the equipment and how it’s used. That doesn’t mean every device on that list will run together for three days. Your combined load determines the runtime.

The Apex 200 also gives you more control over where that energy goes. Four independently controllable Smart AC outlets built right into the unit – no need to buy smart plugs! – let you switch individual devices on and off through the BLUETTI App, set schedules, and apply state-of-charge controls. So if something doesn’t need power overnight, you can turn off its power at the outlet and save the fridge’s battery.

BLUETTI calls the feature an industry first for portable power stations. The system also works with Amazon Alexa, Google Home, and Home Assistant.

A UPS function switches connected equipment to battery power in 15 milliseconds. Check that switching time against your equipment’s requirements, especially for a CPAP or other sensitive device.

With AC output on and the display off, idle consumption drops to just 10.5W.

A winter freeze or severe storm can leave you without grid power for days. That’s when adding extra storage starts to make more sense.

For typical power outages, adding one or two BLUETTI B300K batteries can extend essential home backup to two to three days.

But you can go further. One Apex 200 supports up to six B500K expansion batteries, bringing its maximum capacity to 33.28kWh.

But a bigger battery still needs recharging eventually. The Apex 200 accepts up to 3kW of solar input across two independent channels:

With a correctly configured array of SORA 500 portable solar panels making full use of those inputs, BLUETTI says the base battery can charge from 0 to 80% in 50 minutes, or reach 100% in 1.7 hours using solar alone.

A solar generator setup lets you recharge during daylight. The Apex 200 can also be charged with wall AC, vehicle charging, and compatible gas-generator charging. A suitable 30A generator connection can help replenish the battery when solar production falls short.

The Apex 200 can also form part of a larger home battery backup system through BLUETTI’s Hub A1 parallel box.

BLUETTI specifies up to 6kW of continuous AC output and approximately 100kWh of storage across a parallel system using up to three Apex 200 units.

That’s a significant increase over the standalone battery, but your daily consumption still matters. A steady 1kW load uses 24kWh in 24 hours. Heavy-draw appliances can make a large battery feel much smaller.

BLUETTI positions its larger configurations for three to four days of essential-panel backup. How close you get depends on your batteries, appliances, and ability to recharge.

If you want automatic backup through your home’s electrical panel, confirm the compatible transfer equipment, supported circuits, voltage, and output for the exact bundle. Those details determine what you can actually keep running.

Start with your most likely outage, then decide whether you need more runtime, a charging source, or both.

Extra batteries extend runtime. Solar panels or another charging source recharge them. For outages that stretch into days, both can be worth having.

When shopping for a camper van or travel trailer, choosing a battery comes down to more than just capacity. Among its 10 output ports are two connections RV owners will appreciate having built in.

The native 30A TT-30R RV outlet plugs directly into travel trailer shore power inlets for 120V power.

The 12V/30A Anderson port can directly power compatible DC equipment, including portable fridges and communications gear. This avoids converting battery power to AC and then back to DC, cutting out unnecessary conversion steps.

For charging between campsites, the system can pair with the BLUETTI Charger 2, which combines alternator and solar charging support. It lets you use driving time to replenish the battery through faster vehicle alternator charging, then use solar when you’re parked.

BLUETTI’s recommended mobile bundle is the Apex 200 + SORA 500 solar panel + Charger 2. You get storage for camp, solar charging during your stay, and alternator charging on the road. Compatible campground AC gives you another option.

The Apex 200 is the better fit if you value a smaller enclosure, easier transport, native RV ports, and a lower upfront cost. You can start with 2.56kWh and expand to 33.28kWh on one unit, or approximately 100kWh across a fully expanded parallel system.

The Apex 300 is worth considering if your priority is higher native output and capacity for a system that will mostly stay at home. It offers 3,840W of output and 2,764.8Wh of battery storage, and BLUETTI positions it for more advanced home backup, including compatible 120V/240V configurations.

For someone who wants a battery for both blackouts and RV trips, the Apex 200’s size and connections make a useful combination. You can buy the storage you need now and add more when your power needs change.

The Apex 200 launches November 4, with the standalone unit starting at $1,099 during the November 4–18 super early-bird promotion.

Founded in 2013, BLUETTI allows millions of users across more than 120 countries to stay safe and prepared. Its in-house R&D supports a range of solar generators and home backup systems for outage preparation, RV travel, and off-grid living and recreation.

Shop the Apex 200 and launch bundles, and use ELECTREK5OFF at checkout for an extra 5% savings.

#4754. Bella Hadid Goes All-In on Colorado With the Purchase of a $5.5 Million Mountain Home

Looks like Bella Hadid is putting down roots in Colorado. On November 10, the Wall Street Journal revealed that the model had spent $5.5 million on a home in Crested Butte, about 20 miles south of Aspen. The news came just a day after Hadid hard-launched her new boyfriend, construction project manager Nathan Lacy, whose connection to the area goes back five generations. According to a statement Hadid’s listing agent gave to the WSJ, she had been living in the region for “several months” before pulling the trigger on her unique new digs, built from two coal miner sheds that date to the early 20th century.

Situated just a few feet from Coal Creek, the 2,000-square-foot residence is complete with three bedrooms and three bathrooms. The sellers built the home in 2001, using two existing structures composed of wood and corrugated metal that had stood on the property for 100 years. The sheds were reassembled over a new foundation, with each wooden plank returned to its exact spot on its wall, according to the WSJ. Antique timber from an old Montana mine makes up the rest of the exterior, while pine reclaimed from an 18th-century Virginia barn lines the floors.

A reverse floor plan was designed to let more light into the upper level common areas, like the fireplace-warmed great room, when snow piles up around the ground floor. Reclaimed warehouse beams from a similar time period to the original structures line the vaulted ceiling, with original iron bolts still in place.

The primary suite, which is set up in one of the original coal sheds on the ground level, is outfitted with a kiva-style fireplace, skylights, a soaking tub, and French doors opening to a flagstone patio overlooking the creek. A separate “bunkhouse” ADU rounds out the property.

It’s easy to see why Hadid—a horse girl through and through—would be drawn to the rustic, Western-style digs.

#4753. 8 Best Travel Pants for Women, Tested by Travel Experts and Editors

You won't be counting down the minutes to take these off.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

My passport book is nearly out of blank pages, and I’m starting to worry that my next trip will require an emergency upgrade to make it through customs. But as a frequent flyer and style writer, one thing I don’t stress over is what to wear to the airport. Between maxing out my PTO and logging plenty of miles for work (including tons of in-transit testing for WH Travel Awards), I’ve mastered the art of the airport fit. And while I firmly believe that wearing jeans on a plane should land you on the no-fly list, I’m all about wearing something comfortable without looking like I’m wearing pajamas at the terminal.

That’s where the right pair of travel pants comes in clutch, hitting that happy medium between polished and comfortable. I’m talking about pants you can sit in for hours, sprint through a terminal in, and still wear straight to dinner without a second thought. Over time (and many, many flights), I’ve narrowed down the pairs that truly deliver: versatile, low-maintenance styles that work just as well in your suitcase as they do on your body, from takeoff to touchdown.

The Vuori Halo Essential Wideleg pant has been at the top of my drawer since I got my first pair nearly a year ago. I’m obsessed with the super-soft and smooth polyester and elastane blend. It feels nearly pajama-like while looking way more polished than your average sweatpant (especially if you opt for a darker color like black or navy).

I often reach for this pant when getting dressed for the airport because I know I’ll be comfortable on the plane and that I’ll wear it at least once during my trip. The wide-leg silhouette skims the body in a really flattering way without looking baggy or oversized. It looks great paired with Vuori’s matching zip-up and my fave Dr. Scholl’s Time Off Sneaker for long-haul flights, but it just as easily dresses up with a cute sandal and a form-fitting tank or tee.

Oh, and the pant never wrinkles. It feels soft and cotton-like but since it's made from a buttery synthetic blend, it always looks sleek—more quiet luxury than airport chaos. The material isn’t too thick either, so I don’t find myself overheating while wearing it, even when I land in a sunny destination. I wore this pant while traveling to Mexico recently and felt totally comfortable from takeoff in New York until I arrived at the hotel.

If you’re looking for an under-$50 find that holds its own against pricier pairs, the Old Navy Linen-Blend Ankle Pant is it. Made from a 55% linen blend, it delivers the airy look and feel you want from linen—without the steep price tag most comparable styles carry.

Comfort-wise, it’s exactly what I want for a travel day: lightweight, breathable, and stylish. The secret is in the fabric. This pant blends linen with rayon, a semi-synthetic fiber derived from natural sources like wood pulp that’s known for being soft, smooth, and less prone to creasing than 100% linen. The result is breezy but cozy fabric that doesn’t feel remotely scratchy or itchy. I also love the clean, straight-leg silhouette and high waist that makes me feel put-together with next to zero effort.

I will say, this is one of those pairs I prefer to wear on the plane rather than pack, since it picks up a few more wrinkles when folded in a suitcase (it is still linen, after all). But once I put it on, the fabric bounces back nicely—and I end up reaching for it constantly throughout my trip. The pant is endlessly versatile: I’ll throw it on with flat sandals and a white tee for daytime exploring, then swap in a blouse and heels for dinner without missing a beat.

If you didn’t know better, you might mistake the lululemon Daydrift High-Rise Wide-Leg Trouser for a lounge pant—but one mirror check and it’s giving Succession-coded energy. It’s my go-to for when I need to land and immediately be “on,” whether that’s heading to a meeting or traveling with colleagues.

Made primarily from nylon and elastane, this pant is breathable, sweat-wicking, and cool to the touch—exactly what I want for a long day on the go. It has a smooth, tailored look that resists wrinkling, making it especially suitcase-friendly. It also features a stretch waistband with an internal drawstring, which makes a big difference when I’m sitting for hours or dealing with the general unpredictability of travel days.

I’ll wear it with my go-to Uniqlo Crew Neck T-Shirt and sneakers for a more casual, on-the-move look, but it just as easily leans corporate with a button-down or blazer. Swap in a silky top and heels and it even holds its own for evening plans. It’s that comfort and versatility that make it such a staple in my everyday and travel wardrobe.

If you want something that feels barely there for a warm-weather vacation, the FP Movement Champ Is Here Pant is my top rec. Made from 100% nylon, it’s airy and flowy and allows for total free range of movement—perfect for long travel days or more active itineraries. And thanks to the barrel-leg silhouette (meaning it’s a bit wider at the knee area) and the subtle contrast piping, it still feels on-trend.

Its nylon construction is naturally lightweight, quick-drying, and impressively durable, which is great if your trip involves anything beyond just walking through airports and lounging around. The water-resistant finish and a reinforced woven design help resist tearing and ripping, so it holds up whether you’re caught in a drizzle, heading out on a hike, or just putting it through its paces. But it still feels soft and breathable—not stiff or overly technical.

“I’m a big fan of track pants, and the second I bought this pair, I had travel in mind,” says associate editor Olivia Luppino. “The open, barrel-leg fit makes it super comfortable and yet fashionable to wear on a plane—and I’ve also worn it on a hike, as a beach cover-up, and even dressed it up for dinner.” I’ve found the same—it looks great with sneakers and a tank for daytime, or a fitted top and sandals for nighttime. The only small caveat is the rise: it does sit quite high, which can feel like a lot if you have a shorter torso (I sometimes fold the waistband down for a more comfortable fit).

If you’ve ever tried to juggle your phone, passport, lip balm, and boarding pass while sprinting through a terminal, you get the value of a pocketed pair of pants. The Athleta Skyline High Rise Barrel Leg Pant is my fave in the category. The deep, secure pockets make a huge difference when I’m on the go and don’t want to constantly dig through my bag like I’m Mary Poppins.

Made from polyester, cotton, and spandex, it has a structured, almost denim-like feel—but with way more stretch. The pant has a polished, slightly tailored look, but with the kind of softness and flexibility that makes long flights and all-day wear far more comfortable. The breathable fabric allows for airflow and quick-drying properties that come in handy if you’re on the move (or caught in less-than-ideal weather). There’s even UPF 40+ protection for extra coverage on sunny days. I sort of think of it as an upgraded cargo pant— functional, but not in a “I just came from REI” kind of way.

The barrel-leg silhouette adds a slightly relaxed shape that still feels put-together, and the material isn’t too bulky. I love that this pant works for air travel, city exploring, light hikes, and casual dinners. The only downside? The slightly more structured fabric means they’re not quite as soft or drapey as some of the other pairs on this list—but I still find the fit super flattering.

I usually don’t wear sweatpants during travel because they read way too casual compared to a jogger or trousers. But for longer flights, I sometimes make an exception—and this is the pair I’ll reach for. The straight-leg silhouette feels a bit more put-together than most other sweatpants, but it’s still super soft and lightweight. This sweatpant looks great with almost any casual fit, but our style team loves wearing it with Alo’s color-coordinating jackets and hoodies for a chic, monochrome vibe.

It’s made with a French terry cloth (a cotton blend that’s smooth on the outside) and stylist Alexandra Juric says this makes for a soft, breathable fleece lining. It has a slightly oversized look, but if you want a more snug fit, you can size down. However, I’m into the oversized look and love that this pair doesn’t fit too tightly on the lower belly, since other popular sweatpants I’ve tested can emphasize that area too much. Style contributor Lily Wohlner also prefers it a bit bigger, as she can always roll down the waistband for a more snug fit around the hips.

“The only downside to these sweats is the length; the pants go well past my ankle, making them hard to wear outside,” says Juric. But, sizing down, rolling the waistband, or wearing a platform sneaker would likely solve that problem.

The Vince Bias Cut High Waist Pant is easily the most stylish pair of travel pants in my rotation. It has a liquid-like drape that instantly makes any outfit feel more luxe and the fit is incredibly flattering. I wore it nonstop on my last trip to Spain—on the plane, out to dinner, even just wandering during the day—and it somehow always looked chic with minimal effort.

It’s made from a blend of acetate (a semi-synthetic fiber derived from wood pulp—known for a silky feel and subtle sheen) and polyester, which gives this pant that drapey fit. The bias cut, which refers to cutting the fabric diagonally across the grain, allows the material to skim the body rather than cling to it, creating a fluid effect that I find super flattering. It also gives the pant a natural stretch and tons of movement, so it doesn’t feel restrictive. Add in the high waist and the range of chic neutrals it comes in and you have a truly classic-looking pant.

During my last trip, I styled this pant with a simple tank and sandals during the day, then swapped in a blouse and heels at night. It packs relatively well, too, thanks to that fluid fabric—and because it’s so lightweight, it doesn’t take up much space in a carry-on. The only downside is the care: it’s hand wash, line dry, which isn’t always the most convenient if you need to freshen up mid-trip.

If comfort is your top priority, the Skims Cotton Jersey Foldover Pant is the softest pair in the lineup. This is the kind of pant I put on for a flight and immediately feel better—like I’m wearing my favorite pajamas but still look pulled together enough to step off the plane without a full outfit change. It’s an ideal pant for long-haul days, early morning departures, or anytime you just want to feel cozy without fully leaning into sleepwear or baggy silhouettes.

It’s made from a jersey blend (mostly cotton with a touch of elastane), which is what gives it that ultra-soft, slightly stretchy feel. Cotton keeps things breathable and gentle against the skin, while elastane adds just enough give for when you’re sitting, walking, or curled up in a window seat. The foldover waistband is a standout feature—it lets you customize the rise depending on your preference, whether you want a more low-slung, relaxed fit or a bit more coverage. The fabric has that smooth, second-skin quality that moves with you, making it especially great for travel days when comfort is non-negotiable.

That said, it’s more versatile than you might expect. I’ll wear it with a simple tank and sneakers for an easy airport look, but it also works with a structured jacket to feel a bit more put-together. It also packs down to almost nothing, making it a great backup option in your carry-on. The one trade-off is that it does lean more casual—so while it’s perfect for the plane and low-key plans, it’s not quite as polished as some of the other options here.

Look for pants made with materials that are:

Packing smarter starts with choosing capsule wardrobe essentials that pull double (or triple) duty—think a crisp button-down that you can wear over a tank or tucked into trousers, a lightweight knit that works on the plane and at dinner, or a simple slip dress that doubles as a beach coverup and dinner outfit. Travel pants should follow that same philosophy: versatile enough to style casually with sneakers and a tee, but polished enough to pair with a blouse or blazer. Building multiple outfits around one reliable piece avoids overpacking and makes dressing while on vacation way easier.

Since studying abroad in 2019, I’ve been traveling nonstop. I’ve visited nearly 30 countries so far (8 last year alone!), and learned exactly which travel clothes are best for packing and wearing on long-haul flights and train rides. Plus, as a style writer for Women’s Health, I also travel for work while scoping out destinations for WH’s Travel Awards. For the past few months, I’ve researched and tested the best travel pants for jet-setting in style and comfort alongside style contributor Lily Wohlner and associate editor Olivia Luppino. In addition to testing pants based on comfort, durability, versatility, and style, I also consulted a travel expert for her guidance.

#4752. To Grow Up, First Grow Down

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 14, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

Our culture likes easy measurements of maturity, such as chronological age, number of achievements, financial stability, and the ability to adapt to conventional norms for having a job and a place to live. However, a person can meet these criteria for growing up and still have little or no psychological maturity. The word maturity comes from the Latin word matures, meaning “ripen.” We can understand ripen as meaning “moving beyond early stages of development.” But before we can ripen, we may need to grow down.

When we grow down, we confront early attitudes and beliefs that strengthen neither our relationship with ourselves nor our relationship with life. Here are a number of these attitudes and beliefs.

Growing down is a process of letting go or dying, where denial and certain attachments are challenged and gradually let go. It often takes multiple acts of letting go before an attachment is released. Let’s look at how the growing down process can translate into ripening or growing up.

Maturity can so often be such a vague concept that we don’t know what it is or whether we can actually influence it. Everyone seems to want to “grow up” into a flourishing adulthood, yet it can help to take “growing down” seriously because it shows us what we need to let go of and get ready for. It's not much different from clearing land of rocks and debris in order to prepare for planting and growing. The goal is to take some of the mystique out of becoming an adult. We owe it to ourselves and to others to attend first to some of our more primitive attitudes before we find ourselves merely pretending we are adults.

#4750. Aniioki A9 Pro Max review: Basically an electric motorcycle that you can pedal

There are electric bikes, there are electric motorcycles, and then there are machines like the Aniioki A9 Pro Max that plant a flag somewhere in the increasingly large no-man’s-land between the two.

Technically, it has pedals. You can pedal it fairly effectively too, with the actually adjustable seat. You can even pedal it for fun, which is more than I can say for some of the increasingly motorcycle-shaped “e-bikes” I’ve tested lately.

But let’s get something out of the way right at the beginning: this isn’t a street-legal electric bicycle in the US. Not when we’re talking about dual motors producing up to 6,000W of peak power and speeds of around 45 mph.

And you know what? That’s fine. As long as we’re all honest about what this thing is.

The Aniioki A9 Pro Max is absolutely massive, and the spec sheet makes that abundantly clear.

The version I tested uses a pair of 2,500W direct-drive hub motors, one in each wheel, with Aniioki claiming 3,000W peak power from each motor. That gives the bike a combined peak figure of 6,000W and up to 250 Nm of combined torque. It’s hard to overstate how massive that is.

Then there’s the battery. You can choose between a 60V 70Ah pack with 4.2 kWh of capacity or an even larger 60V 80Ah pack packing 4.8 kWh. For comparison, many typical commuter e-bikes have somewhere around 500-700 Wh of battery. The smaller battery here is roughly six to eight times that size. That’s absolutely in the territory of legit light electric motorcycles.

Aniioki claims up to 230+ miles (370 km) of pedal-assist range, though as usual, you should take maximum e-bike range figures as best-case numbers. Using the throttle and enjoying those big motors is going to dramatically reduce that figure. Even so, with more than 4 kWh of battery underneath you, range anxiety isn’t exactly the first thing that comes to mind.

All that hardware comes with a predictable penalty: weight. The 70Ah model tips the scales at around 188 lb (85 kg), while the 80Ah version approaches 193 lb (87.5 kg). Those aren’t e-bike weights. Those are motorcycle weights. Again, you can see the direction this is going.

Here’s where the A9 Pro Max gets more interesting to me.

A lot of high-powered e-motos include pedals seemingly as a regulatory fig leaf. They’re technically there, but the geometry is so bad that nobody in their right mind would want to pedal the thing farther than across a parking lot. Even some smaller and presumably Class 2 legal e-bikes that have moto-style frames are nearly unpedalable for actual riding over any reasonable distance.

But the A9 here is actually pedalable thanks to having something that more closely resembles a bicycle seat, plus adjustability that lets riders dial in the correct seat height.

The A9 Pro Max feels more like a strange combination of an oversized fat-tire e-bike and a small electric motorcycle. There’s a Shimano 7-speed drivetrain and a huge 72-tooth chainring, meaning the pedals aren’t entirely ornamental.

I actually enjoyed pedaling it with the pedal assist engaged. You’re obviously not going to mistake a nearly 200-pound machine rolling on enormous 26 x 4.8-inch tires for a lightweight fitness bike, but there’s something fun about contributing some human power while two giant hub motors do most of the heavy lifting.

And when you don’t feel like pedaling, there’s a full-twist throttle waiting for you.

That combination is really the appeal here. You can ride it more like an e-bike when the mood strikes, or twist the throttle and treat it more like a lightweight e-moto.

And again, I don’t want to beat a dead horse here, but remember: the pedals don’t make this an electric bicycle. It’s still an e-moto, but it’s one that you can actually have fun pedaling. You can treat it like a mech suit, where pedaling translates into crazy power, as if you have super-human legs. And with the insanely large 72t chainring, pedaling at higher speeds is actually doable. Though I’ll tell you right now, pedaling at 40 mph (64 km/h) is not exactly a normal or natural feeling.

And it’s worth pointing out that at a starting price of US $2,899 (or more for the larger battery capacities), that’s a fairly reasonable price compared to most e-motos that can be more limiting in how and where you can ride them.

Fortunately, Aniioki seems to understand that putting this much power on two wheels requires more serious components than the average bicycle.

The braking setup is particularly wild. There are two massive 300mm brake rotors on the front wheel and another 300mm rotor out back, along with a linked CBS braking system. The front uses custom eight-piston calipers (the pair of quad-piston calipers) while the rear gets a custom six-piston setup.

There’s also an adjustable air-suspension fork with 110mm of travel, rear suspension to smooth out bumps at higher speeds, integrated lighting and turn signals, and a large five-inch display that even incorporates features like Bluetooth audio and a recording camera.

That brings us to the elephant in the room.

In the US, consumer-product rules generally define a low-speed electric bicycle around a motor of less than 750W and a maximum motor-powered speed below 20 mph (32 km/h), while individual states use their own operating laws that typically match the familiar Class 1/2/3 framework. A 6,000W machine capable of around 45 mph (72 km/h) blows straight through normal limits.

So please don’t see pedals and assume this belongs on your local bicycle path.

Where and how you can legally operate something like the A9 Pro Max depends on your local laws and whether it can qualify under another vehicle category. For many owners, the sensible place to enjoy its full performance is going to be private property or other areas where such vehicles are permitted.

That caveat doesn’t make the bike itself bad. It just means buyers need to understand what they’re buying.

And judged on what it actually is rather than what the word “e-bike” on the product page suggests, I had a lot of fun on it.

There are certainly riders who would look at a nearly 200-pound, 45 mph machine and say, “Why not just buy an electric motorcycle?” That’s a perfectly reasonable question.

In addition to kW power limits, the legal boundary for what is an e-bike should also include weight. Anything over 100lbs including battery is no longer an e-bike and it carries a dangerous amount of momentum once it is cruising. 190 lbs is ridiculous.

But I also understand the appeal of this weird middle ground. The A9 Pro Max retains enough bicycle DNA that you can pedal it around and enjoy pedal assist, yet has enough battery and motor underneath you to deliver something much closer to small-motorcycle performance when you twist the throttle.

Imagine going off-road and getting to fly up hills while pedaling hard, but then being able to switch to throttle once your legs get worn out. Sure, it’s not everyone’s cup of tea, but it’s a cup of tea.

This bike is big. It’s heavy. It’s absurdly powerful by e-bike standards. And it absolutely isn’t the machine I’d recommend for someone looking for a normal street-legal electric bicycle.

But if what you actually want is a big, powerful electric two-wheeler that still lets you turn the pedals when the mood strikes, the Aniioki A9 Pro Max makes a surprisingly compelling argument for this increasingly bizarre category of pedal-equipped e-motos.

Encapsulation lifts, cradles, and separates your girls while still eliminating boob bounce. It can be found in the Beyond Yoga bra. #4748. DeepWay electric semi arrives in New Zealand, and gets a new name

New Zealand’s Foodstuffs North Island Limited has given its latest electric semi truck an electrifying new identity, courtesy of a second-grade student at a local elementary school.

The Chinese-built DeepWay Star began delivering chilled and frozen groceries across New Zealand’s lower North Island earlier this year – and, after a naming competition organized with students at Russell Street School in Palmerston North, the big HD EV has got a new name: Evie.

The winning name came from Year 2 (read: second grade) student named Madison, who beat out suggestions including Buzzy Bee, Lightning, and Bolt. Madison got to officially unveil the truck’s new name alongside her classmates, local officials and Foodstuffs representatives.

“Our trucks are out on the road every day delivering food to stores and communities, so we thought it would be great to get the kids involved and give our first electric truck a bit of personality,” explains Foodstuffs North Island General Manager Supply Chain, Yang Zhang. “There were some brilliant ideas, but Evie was a pretty fitting name for an EV. The best part is knowing Madison and the other students will be able to spot Evie out on the road and know they played a part in it.”

Madison was allowed to do the unveiling honors, revealing Evie’s new name alongside her other classmates, Palmerston North’s Mayor, Grant Smith, local MP Tangi Utikeri, and local PAK’nSAVE, New World, and Four Square grocers who will be receiving deliveries from Evie.

In its first few months on the road, Evie’s travelled nearly 45,000 kilometers (~28,000 miles) and avoided more than 81,000 kg of harmful carbon emissions – which the company claims is roughly equivalent to taking 35 ICE cars off the road for a full year.

As for the truck itself, it has a sort of Tesla-ish, anteater-y look, and significantly longer range than the StarWay, offering more than 500 km (~310 miles) of range from its 600 kWh CATL-built LFP battery packs that can plug into charge ports two at a time for lickety-quick charging in about 30 minutes. If that’s too long of a wait, the Star can swap its tired batteries for fresh ones in special battery-sway stations in just six minutes.

The DeepWay’s electric motors put out 491 kW (~660 hp) of power, and a positively tectonic 75,000 (!) Nm (~55,000 lb-ft) (!!) of torque – more than enough to get the 50 tons (100,000 lb.) of GVWR it’s rated for up to speed.

It is great to see electric trucks replacing Diesel. I just can’t understand why EV adoption is so slow to take off in New Zealand. It has plenty of great low cost EVs and petrol is all imported and expensive.

You can check out the pictures, above, then let us know what you think of the big Chinese BEV and it’s fun new name in the comments.

#4747. Bunny Williams Never Set Out to Collect Birdhouses—Now a Whole Village of Them Stands in Her Connecticut Garden

Among the apple trees at the edge of AD100 Hall of Famer Bunny Williams’s storied country garden in Falls Village, Connecticut, stands a church with a sensible tin roof; a thatched cottage; a pagoda; a red house flying a tiny flag that she takes for a general store; and a shuttered confection that suggests a Russian dacha. Each is raised high on its own post, finished on every side, painted and weathered like the structures of a settled town—and none has a door you could fit a hand through. It is a hamlet fashioned for birds, assembled building by building, the way real towns often grow: slowly, and without a master plan.

For many years as Williams and her husband, the antiques dealer John Rosselli, combed fields and fairs for Treillage, the much-loved shop they ran in New York City until 2015, the birdhouses kept finding her. They gathered on shelves in the hayloft of her barn. “When I had two, I didn’t know what to do with them,” she says. “Then all of a sudden there were 10.” She decided they had been in storage long enough.

A farmhouse with a side porch crafted by the late Larry Smith, a North Georgia birdhouse builder known for fashioning charmingly detailed structures with metal roofs.

An A-frame house embellished with gingerbread trim and decorative brackets

Williams, on a tree stump next to the pagoda. The notch in the base of the birdhouse indicates that it was probably designed to be mounted on a roof.

At that point, Williams and Robert Reimer, head gardener on her property, started the process of reclaiming a long-overlooked point of land. To create space and liberate a stand of existing apple trees, they removed invasive species, then planted oat grass, bird-friendly scrub plants, and fruit-bearing pawpaw trees. To create the neighborhood, she had uniform posts made—tall, “so that you look up at them,” each wrapped with a metal band to deter ambitious squirrels from climbing too high and disturbing the tenants she had in mind. Finally, up went the houses, now totaling 17.

The attraction had nothing to do with value or pedigree. “Most of these birdhouses are sort of folk art,” she says. “They were somebody having fun building an unusual structure.” Not Monticello in miniature, not a replica of someone’s own house, just unknown makers, each with “an eye and a kind of humor,” none of them trying to be perfect. The proof is in the details: the gingerbread scallops on one many-holed high-rise (“somebody had a great time with their little saw”), the thatched-roof cottage she prizes because she has never seen another like it, the weather vane crowning the would-be dacha.

A church with a brick chimney, an oversized cupola, and Gothic Revival design elements.

A rare combination house and feeder that evokes a neoclassical temple

Williams calls this one the general store.

A colonial revival house with a columned portico built by Larry Smith

“It has a kind of Russian dacha feeling,” says Williams.

What she didn’t have was history—the dealers who sold them seldom had any to pass along. The record, it turns out, is often recoverable. “The period from 1890 to 1930 is really the birdhouse’s golden age,” says Jacob Torkelson, an architectural historian and researcher at the University of Pennsylvania’s Stuart Weitzman School of Design, and among the very few scholars in the country studying these objects, whose makers and manufacturers he has painstakingly been identifying, where a name survives. Across those decades, government pattern books encouraged farmers to install birdhouses to reduce pesticide use (the birds would eat the insects), while mail-order companies offered them to homeowners as pure whimsy, not to mention a way of promoting biodiversity in their gardens. Shown photographs of Williams’s collection, Torkelson supplied some of what the dealers couldn’t. He traced one house down to the catalog page: the six-room Bungalow Martin House sold by the E.F. Hodgson Company, which listed the model from about 1917 until the firm closed in 1944. “Birdhouses are these wonderful mirrors to the human condition,” Torkelson says. “They tell us the values that we have as a society or as individuals, in our houses, in our gardens.”

A double porch house also built by Larry Smith

This pagoda-inspired birdhouse provides multiple roosting spots.

An unusual thatched-roof cottage prized by Williams, who has never seen another like it.

Williams isn’t finished collecting. Last May at Trade Secrets, the annual Litchfield Hills garden fair she cofounded in 2001 to raise funds for a local nonprofit domestic violence support agency, she stopped at the tent of Jim Sidon, whose company, Sparrow 10:29, crafts avian-size replicas of real buildings. Sidon, based outside Atlanta, came to the work after retiring from the printing industry. His first architectural birdhouse, built in 2017, was a replica of the 1792 Federal-style mansion in Newburyport, Massachusetts, where he and his wife had rented two rooms as newlyweds. It was Sidon who recognized, in three of Williams’s houses, the hand of his late friend Larry Smith, a North Georgia birdhouse builder known for his metal roofs and charmingly rustic details. Williams has asked Sidon to build her something new, though she is still deciding exactly what. Unlike her anonymous makers, Sidon numbers and signs every house. “My hope is that years from now, someone’s searching that out,” he says, “and when they open it up, they’ll see my signature.”

A dovecote-inspired birdhouse offers multiple residences

A picturesque house topped with a prominent weather vane

Drawing the eye like miniature garden follies, the houses rise on poles amid a stand of apple trees from ground planted with oat grass and bird-friendly scrub plants.

In Falls Village, the upkeep routine is minimal: Every couple of years the houses come down, receive a coat of wood preservative, and go back up into the weather. Sidon’s constructions, with cedar exteriors and sealed against the elements, ask even less. His replica of the Newburyport house has stood in his own garden for nearly a decade untouched. “I just hose it off,” he says. None of this troubles Torkelson, a preservationist by training. “These houses were made to be ephemeral,” he says. “They weren’t made to last forever, and they should absolutely be used.”

As for the intended residents? Williams thinks the birds mostly prefer making their homes in the trees, where they carry on, she says, like a symphony orchestra: “I’ve always felt that one of the reasons they don’t live in these houses is the birds think it’s suburbia. But they like the atmosphere.” Come winter, when the woods go bare and the village shows through the branches, Sidon would bet the houses do get used, songbirds crowding in two and three at a time for warmth. Williams can’t say—she has never once climbed up to look. “If they are nesting,” she says, “I don’t want to bother them.”

#4746. I Was Making an Important Point, but Now It’s Gone

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 14, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

Have you ever been in a situation where you knew exactly what you wanted to talk about, but when the moment arrived, you couldn’t think of what you had planned to say?

That’s what happened to Jen* when she made her first big presentation at a new job. She practiced the talk repeatedly, to the point at which she felt confident that she could make it without a mistake. Yet when a senior colleague interrupted her to ask her to clarify what she had just said, her brain went blank.

“I felt so stupid,” she said. “It was a simple question. I knew the answer. But my mind left the room. My brain froze completely.”

Many factors can contribute to this kind of “brain freeze,” which fits into a category of cognitive problems called “word retrieval difficulties.” There are a number of possible causes, both physiological and psychological, but there is also the odd and amazing role of unconscious dynamics that can make our brains stop working just when we need them to work at top capacity.

The brain is a complex organ that controls thought, memory, emotion, touch, motor skills, vision, breathing, temperature, hunger, and every process that regulates our body. When any of these factors is in play, the complex system of neurons through which the brain stores and recovers words may not be firing as quickly as you would like.

Anxiety—already a complex emotion—can be a lot more complicated when unconscious thoughts and feelings play a role. These are thoughts and feelings that go on outside of our awareness. They are often behind behaviors that we can’t explain to ourselves.

For instance, Jen’s brain freeze during her presentation could certainly have been caused by her anxiety about proving herself to her new colleagues and bosses. But contributing to her anxiety may have been some thoughts and feelings that she kept hidden away, even from herself. It’s very hard for us to uncover these hidden emotions on our own, because we push them out of our minds and into what Freud called the “unconscious” mind.

Today we think of these ideas as “split off” or “dissociated” from awareness.

The psychoanalyst Christopher Bollas gave the name “unthought known” to the thoughts and feelings, memories, and ideas about ourselves that we don’t let ourselves know about.

Sometimes we relegate information, without realizing it, to the unknown part of ourselves, to protect ourselves from old, painful memories. But we can also use this powerful tool to step away from a side of ourselves that we don’t like. This emotional process almost always happens outside of our awareness.

The presence of unconscious thoughts and feelings does not necessarily rule out physiological causes for memory loss. If it happens to you on a regular basis, it may still not be a cause for concern, but it’s important to have a medical professional check to make sure it’s not a symptom of a medical problem.

If this type of memory loss happens only on occasion, even if you aren’t in psychotherapy, you can start to look for some patterns that reveal unconscious reasons for behaviors and feelings that you can’t explain. And once you understand what’s going on behind the scenes in your psyche, it’s much easier to do something about it.

If you consistently go blank at work, for example, you can start to track the specific moments when it happens. When do you forget? Is it with a particular person or group of people? Does it happen in certain situations?

As Jen began to sort through some of her unacknowledged thoughts and feelings about the presentation, she realized that she was not only trying to prove herself to her new colleagues, but also secretly trying to prove to her family how well she was doing.

She wanted to impress them, particularly her father and her older sister. “I imagined telling them how well I had done,” she said. “I love the expression on my dad’s face when he tells me he’s proud of me. But that’s something I know and think about all the time. Maybe I’m too much of a daddy’s girl.”

After a few minutes of talking and thinking, Jen said, “I think maybe part of the problem is that a secret part of me also wanted to make my sister feel bad. She always does well at everything, and I’m always feeling like I can’t quite match up to her. I wanted her to feel the same way for once.”

As Jen talked about this dynamic with her sister, something she knew but did not like to think about, she had to face her competitiveness head-on. “It’s something I don’t like about myself,” she said. “I mean, it’s OK to be competitive. But it’s not OK to want to hurt the person you’re competing with. It makes me feel so bad about myself.”

We suspected that Jen had shut down just as she was beginning to show off. Of course, we can’t know, but it seemed likely that her internal dialogue connected showing off at work with a wish to hurt her sister by rubbing her success in. Because Jen was so critical of this part of herself, she may have shut it down, stopping her brain in the process.

Once we had talked out the meaning of Jen’s brain fog, we began to explore Jen’s competition with her sister. It had many different components, and it took a while, but eventually Jen realized that she could succeed without hurting her sister. The next time she made a presentation, she did not fog up.

It’s not always easy to know what your unconscious mind is thinking. But if you decide to do some internal exploration, start with the idea that the "unthought known" is something you don’t like about yourself. Once you’ve located the difficult thoughts, it’s easier to change your behavior. And the “unthought known” is much less likely to sabotage you.

#4745. The 10 Most Comfortable Bras, According to Style Editors

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

I’ve tested more bras than I can count as a style writer. And over the years, I’ve learned that comfort is a nonnegotiable—if it digs, pinches, or rides up, it doesn’t deserve a space in my drawer. The thing is, no two boobs are exactly alike (not even your own). One might sit higher, be fuller, or have a different shape than the other. So finding the right bra isn’t about hitting a standard size—it’s about understanding your body. According to Navya Mysore, MD, a primary care physician and Women’s Health advisor, the right bra boosts comfort, improves posture, and eases back pain by evenly distributing breast tissue. If your band rides up, your straps slide, or your underwire doesn’t lie flat, it’s a clear sign something’s off.

And if your usual size suddenly stops working? Totally normal. Bra fitter and undergarment educator Kimmay Caldwell says weight changes, hormone shifts, or your monthly cycle can impact your size. To make it trickier, some brands still use outdated sizing methods (like the “plus four” rule), while others go by your exact underbust. Bottom line: your size can change and vary between clothing brands.

All of that can make bra shopping feel like a bit of a minefield, which is exactly why I tested 20 different styles across fits, fabrics, and support levels to find the ones that are actually worth your money. These ten passed the wear test and then some, proving that comfort, support, and style actually can exist in one bra.

A bra should fit your body—not the other way around—and Knix totally got the memo with this one. It feels snug at first, but it softens and molds to your shape with every wear. What really impressed me was the fit because it almost feels custom, thanks to the ultra-thin foam that contours without adding volume.

Plus, the sleek fabric (a nylon-spandex blend) moves with you, feeling super smooth against the skin and breathable enough to wear for hours.

If you're after definition without the discomfort, this wire-free option def delivers. The molded cups lift and separate, while subtle side padding helps prevent spillage and sideboob. The result? A natural shape, no extra bulk, and no awkward lines under tighter tops. And with 99 sizes (!!) and eight colors, the options are actually inclusive.

The only downside? It’s not the best for high movement and workouts. I find myself adjusting it when I bend or move quickly. Still, for everyday comfort and a super flattering fit, this one’s a standout.

If you love the shape and support of a traditional bra but can't stand the feel of underwire, the Shapermint Essentials Sweetheart Wireless Contour Bra is your happy medium. It delivers a surprisingly lifted, rounded silhouette without a single wire digging into your ribs, making it my top pick for anyone who wants all-day comfort.

The lightly contoured foam cups provide just enough structure to prevent the dreaded uniboob, while the wide, stretchy band stays comfortably in place without pinching or rolling. The smooth, buttery fabric feels soft against the skin and disappears nicely under T-shirts and other fitted tops.

I was especially impressed by how supportive it feels for a wireless bra. It lifts and shapes without feeling restrictive, and the wider straps help distribute weight so your shoulders don't pay the price after hours of wear. It's one of those bras you forget you're wearing—which is pretty much the highest compliment I can give.

Push-up bras with underwires have a bad rep, and for good reason. They’re usually stiff, pokey, and downright uncomfortable. But after wearing this Maidenform bra for months (yes, months), I can confidently say it’s a major exception to the rule.

From the start, this bra felt different. The underwire doesn’t dig or jab, thanks to its soft, stretchy crochet lace that moves with you. The cups are unpadded but still offer that ideal medium support and lift, enough to give shape and a gentle push-up effect, but never so much that I feel squeezed or overly sculpted. It’s supportive without being suffocating, which is rare in the world of push-ups.And let’s talk about the straps. They’re fully adjustable and convertible, so whether I’m going for a classic or criss-cross fit, I can tweak the style to match my outfit. That kind of versatility makes it feel like you’re getting two bras in one (and who doesn’t love a multitasker?).The lift it gives is subtle but effective. It’s not the dramatic “hello, cleavage” kind of push-up, but more of a natural, perky boost that works under everything from tees to low-cut dresses. No spillage, just a flattering shape that makes me feel more confident in whatever I’m wearing. Bonus points for the range of styles: It comes in smooth fabric options to wear under clingy tees, and lace versions for when you want to have a little more fun.One of my biggest bra fears? The dreaded back and side bulge. But this bra’s smoothing side panels genuinely help—there’s no weird digging or over-compression, just a smooth, flattering fit that doesn’t fight with your body. Long story short: I tested it, I lived in it, and I’m keeping it in my regular rotation.

The soft, stretchy fabric, made from a smooth microfiber that consists of 85 percent polyamide and 15 percent elastane, molds to your body, starting snug and quickly adapting for a custom-like fit. “I will say, mine have stretched a bit over the past few years, so it might be time to re-up,” she says.

This bra provides exceptional support for larger busts, even without a heavy-duty wire band. Instead, it makes use of an elasticized band that provides a surprisingly large amount of support without digging into the skin. It also has extra support at the sides to prevent spillage and to keep everything looking seamless, even under thin t-shirts and tight dresses.

The adjustable straps and underband stay put, and the side coverage smooths everything out—no spillage, no weird lines under shirts. It gives a natural, rounded shape that works under pretty much anything.

If you tend to scoop the girls into place to make them look perkier (a good trick!), this Cuup bra does the work for you. The rounded neckline and unlined, unpadded cups naturally lift and shape, while seamlessly extending into the straps for clean lines and a flattering fit.

It runs snug, but that’s what makes it so supportive—my boobs stay put and look perkier without any adjusting. The nylon and spandex blend feels soft and wearable for hours without digging into your skin while providing a completely seamless silhouette from every angle. I always wear this pick under thinner tops, tight dresses, and clingy sweaters because it creates a totally streamlined look under clothes while lifting the girls and supporting the underarm area and sides.

Plus, the bonded cradle under the bust mimics the structure of an underwire, delivering firm support without any poking or pinching. The full mesh overlay adds light compression and lift, adding to the sleek look.

“The CrossOver bra feels like a sports bra on, which is especially handy for women in search of something extra-comfortable (hi),” says contributor Korin Miller, who wore this bra every day for nearly a month to see how well it performed. This bra also has one of the widest size ranges on our list, which is a major win. However, it does run a little big, so if you're between sizes, consider sizing down for the best fit.

Despite having zero padding, the cups still provide full nipple coverage, so you get a sleek look under even the clingiest t-shirts without adding extra bulk.

I also appreciate that the plunge neckline works under just about everything, from V-necks to lower-cut tops, while the underwire offers just enough lift to create a naturally rounded shape. The result is polished and supportive without looking overly structured.

The only drawback is that it's best suited to smaller busts, as it doesn't offer the level of coverage or support many fuller busts need. But it is available up to a G cup if you’d like to try it out yourself.

If you love a deep V-neckline but hate when your bra peeks out, meet your new go-to: the Harper Wilde Bliss Triangle Bralette. It’s made with a flattering plunge that stays supportive and hidden under low-cut tops and dresses. I’ve worn it under everything from wrap dresses to tanks and it disappears under all of them. The triangle shape gives a natural lift—no wires, no padding, just your boobs but sliiightly perkier.

Comfort-wise, it lives up to the name. The modal fabric is buttery-soft and stretchy in that live-in-it kind of way. The band is wide and smooth, so it stays put without digging, and the adjustable straps let you customize the fit. It’s also lightweight enough to forget you’re even wearing it.

It’s become my go-to for daily wear, and the super-soft, barely-there material is truly the next best thing to going bra-free. While it’s equally great for bed-rotting or taking Zoom calls from home, I also feel confident wearing it out and about because it doesn’t skimp on coverage and offers just enough support.

Even without padding, the double-layered fabric gives solid nipple coverage. It comes in inclusive sizes and neutral shades that go with everything. The few cons? It’s not super supportive for heavy movement or fuller busts, so you may need to readjust on the go. But for everyday wear, especially with low-cut outfits, it fits the bill.

The most comfortable bras usually come down to the right blend of fabrics. Here’s what each one brings to the table:

Comfort is about more than just size—it’s also about ensuring the wire doesn’t create pressure points or cause discomfort throughout the day. Look for bras with flexible, padded, or cushioned underwires, which offer support without digging into your skin. The underwire should sit flat against your ribcage and follow the natural curve of your breasts. If it feels like it’s poking or shifting, it’s not the right fit. If you prefer a wire-free bra, opt for styles with flexible boning, molded cups, and wide, flexible bands to provide support.

The most accurate way to find your size is to get fitted in person. Once you have your size, your new bra should feel snug and secure. The band should be comfortably tight, but not dig into the skin. A good rule of thumb is that you should be able to fit two fingers between the band and your skin, but no more. The cups should also lie flat against your chest.

The Women’s Health team has been testing bras since we first wrote this story in 2023. To find the most comfortable options, our team wore each style for at least a few weeks at a time. We wore them under different circumstances, including workouts, lounging, and long days at the office. But our main criterion for each bra was comfort. I also spoke with two bra experts and personally tested 20-plus bras over several years to lock down the ones I actually wear on repeat.

I recently re-tested a bunch of options and tapped style contributor Lily Wohlner for an update to this story to boost our list and keep it up-to-date. The final guide includes everything from bralettes and seamless bras to push-up bras—and I actually wear all of them in my day-to-day life.

#4744. Electric cars are about to overtake petrol in the UK, data shows

Battery-electric cars took 32% of the UK’s new car market in October, while petrol cars fell to just 37.2%, according to new data from the SMMT. That’s the closest the two have been.

At the current pace, electric cars will outsell petrol in the UK within a year. And it could happen as soon as this December.

The UK registered 152,730 new cars in October, up 5.4% year-over-year and the 11th straight month of growth for the overall market.

All of that growth came from plug-ins. BEV registrations jumped 32.7% to 48,858 units, and plug-in hybrids rose 30.1% to 22,898. Meanwhile, petrol fell 11.6% to 56,876 units, diesel dropped 15.9%, and even conventional hybrids were down 5%.

Through the first 10 months of the year, the UK has now registered 503,805 BEVs, up 30.4%, for a 26.6% market share. Petrol’s year-to-date share is down to 41.1%, from 47.2% at the same point last year.

We pulled SMMT’s monthly fuel-type data going back to March 2024 to see where this is heading. Note that SMMT counts mild hybrids as petrol (or diesel) in its headline categories, and that’s generally how we count them at Electrek.

In March 2024, petrol held 55.9% of the market and BEVs 15.2%. In October 2026, it was 37.2% vs 32.0%. Petrol’s share is shrinking by about half a point per month on a linear trend, while BEVs gain about 0.36 points a month. Extend both lines and they cross around August 2027 at roughly 33% each.

But that’s the slow scenario, because it ignores December.

UK BEV share spikes every December as automakers push volume to get closer to their ZEV Mandate targets. BEVs hit 31.0% in December 2024 and 32.2% in December 2025, when petrol was at 39.4%. Over the last five months, BEV share has run about 5 points higher than a year earlier, and petrol about 7 points lower. If December follows that pattern, BEVs land around 37% and petrol around 32%.

That would be the first time BEVs beat petrol in SMMT’s headline numbers, mild hybrids included.

However, SMMT’s own forecast of 27.2% BEV share for the full year implies roughly 31% for November and December combined, which would make it a much closer call. And on a stricter definition that puts mild hybrids with hybrids instead of petrol, BEVs already outsold every other powertrain in August.

Zoom out to full years and the picture is just as clear. Cars that run only on petrol or diesel, mild hybrids included, made up 72.5% of the UK market in 2021. This year, they’re at 45.5%.

None of this is good enough for the SMMT, which is using the release to push the government, again, to cut the ZEV Mandate targets.

The mandate requires 33% of 2026 sales to be zero-emission. SMMT now forecasts 27.2%. It expects 32% next year against a 38% target, and 37.5% in 2028 against 52%, a 14.5-point gap.

The trade group says automakers have spent “billions” on discounts, 0% financing, deposit contributions, and even subsidized charging to move EVs, on top of the government’s Electric Car Grant. It also slammed last week’s Budget, which confirmed a new EV-specific road tax (eVED) starting in 2028 and kept 20% VAT on public charging.

“Higher targets may force supply, but they do not create demand,” SMMT chief executive Mike Hawes said.

We’ve heard this one before. The SMMT made the same argument after September’s record 99,199 BEV registrations, and the government already opened a review of the mandate this year.

This might be the main reason why the trade group wants to slow things down. The brands growing fastest in the UK are mostly Chinese. BYD registered 6,065 cars in October, up 73%. Jaecoo more than doubled to 6,089 units, Chery nearly tripled to 3,707, and Leapmotor doubled to 1,773. MG was up 85%.

Tesla, on the other hand, registered just 282 cars in October, down 45% from 511 a year ago. The first month of the quarter is always slow for Tesla in the UK, and the brand is still up 31% year-to-date at 46,526 units after a big September. But it didn’t have a single model in October’s top 10 BEVs, which was led by the Skoda Enyaq (1,568), Mini Countryman (1,494), and Jaecoo 5 (1,465).

The SMMT’s framing is that there’s a “demand gap.” The data shows the opposite. BEV registrations are up 30% this year while petrol is shrinking every single month. That’s not a market rejecting EVs.

The SMMT is not a neutral organisation, they have been briefing against EVs for years and continue to do so.

The ZEV mandate is NOT a measure of how many pure BEVs are sold, and the SMMT know it, it's a measure of REDUCING emission against a level set in the past.

Those emissions reductions can be met by selling BEVs, or selling more efficient PHEVs or even selling more efficient petrol or diesel cars! The manufacturers can also buy credits if they choose to.

NO manufacturer has paid any ZEV fines to date (DfT announcement March 2026)

As for the "heavy discounts" and "loss making sales", well I have two data points on that.

1. The retail price of EVs has continued to climb in the UK over the past 6 years, despite the cost of any average 50kWh battery pack dropping several thousand dollars.

2. There are hundreds of main dealerships who are buying cars from the manufacturers, driving them for the minimum 3 month period, often with just a few thousand miles on the clock and then selling them with a 30-35% retail price discount, and then repeating ad infinitum. The dealerships are still making a few thousand with each transaction, so we know where the manufacturers price really sits.

And the discounts automakers keep complaining about? That’s the mandate doing exactly what it was designed to do. It forces automakers to sell EVs, so they price them to sell, and buyers respond. Hawes says targets don’t create demand, but cheaper EVs clearly do. October proves it.

Now, is the jump to 52% in 2028 steep? It is steep, but it looks achievable to me. If anything is hurting demand, it’s the government’s own moves: a new EV-only road tax and 20% VAT on public charging. That’s what the industry should be fighting. It’s too early for that.

Either way, petrol’s days as the UK’s default car are numbered. The only question is whether the milestone comes in December or sometime in 2027. Our bet is December.

#4743. The 9 Most Beautiful States in the US

The most beautiful states in the US prove just how shockingly diverse the country is: volcanic beaches, glacier-capped peaks, canyon-carved deserts, and misty rainforests define their landscapes. What people have built in those places is just as varied, from a royal palace in downtown Honolulu to Mary Colter’s stone watchtower on the rim of the Grand Canyon to the cedar-shingled studios of a modernist craft school on the coast of Maine. These nine states stand out on both counts, for the scenery that defines them and the architecture that holds its own against it. Keep in mind that no ranking can settle which state is most beautiful—they’re all worthy of a visit.

Hawaii is far from a monolithic state, with scenery changing from island to island. In Honolulu on Oahu, ʻIolani Palace, completed in 1882 for King Kalākaua, is the only royal palace on US soil—and it had electricity before the White House did.

Near Diamond Head, Doris Duke’s oceanfront estate, Shangri La, pairs 1930s modernism with architectural elements she brought from Morocco, Iran, Syria, and beyond. It’s now a museum of Islamic art, with tours departing from the Honolulu Museum of Art.

As for the natural landscape, Kauai, known as the Garden Isle, is home to the Nā Pali Coast, where green ridges drop sharply toward the Pacific. On Maui, Haleakalā’s broad volcanic summit often rises above a blanket of clouds. And on the Big Island, Hawaii Volcanoes National Park actively showcases the raw power of volcanoes—if you’re lucky, you might even catch an eruption.

Wyoming’s most famous photo moment might be the Teton Range rising abruptly above the sagebrush flats of Jackson Hole, ideally with one of Mormon Row’s weathered homestead barns in the foreground. Nearby, the tiny log Chapel of the Transfiguration, built in 1925, was sited so that the picture window behind its altar frames the peaks where stained glass would normally go.

In Yellowstone National Park, it’s all about color: Grand Prismatic Spring’s vivid rings stand out among the forested landscape, while the Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone exposes ochres and pinks in its steep walls. And steps from its namesake geyser, the Old Faithful Inn—designed by a 29-year-old Robert Reamer and opened in 1904—wraps a soaring lodgepole-pine lobby around a massive stone fireplace. It’s considered the largest log structure in the world.

Florida’s beaches are perhaps the state’s most scenic draw, but the architecture is just as distinctive. In 1979, Miami Beach’s Art Deco District, roughly a square mile of South Beach, became the nation’s first urban 20th-century historic district on the National Register, with more than 800 buildings listed. Across Biscayne Bay, industrialist James Deering’s Vizcaya, a villa completed in 1916, faces the water with formal gardens by Diego Suarez. Addison Mizner gave Palm Beach its Mediterranean Revival look; his Via Mizner, a winding pedestrian lane off Worth Avenue built in 1923, survives today.

St. Augustine, founded by the Spanish in 1565, pairs the coquina-stone Castillo de San Marcos with Henry Flagler’s Hotel Ponce de Leon, a Spanish Renaissance–style palace from 1888 that’s now Flagler College. Architecture buffs should detour to Lakeland, where Frank Lloyd Wright’s campus for Florida Southern College is the largest single-site collection of his architecture in the world. And on the Gulf Coast, Sarasota’s midcentury modernists adapted the International Style to the subtropics, most famously in Paul Rudolph’s 1953 Umbrella House.

On Maine’s coast, Acadia National Park packs a surprising amount of scenery into a small area: granite headlands, spruce forest, offshore islands, and views of the Atlantic. Look closely, and you'll notice the park’s impressive stonework, too. John D. Rockefeller Jr. financed its network of carriage roads, built between 1913 and 1940, along with 16 of the 17 stone-faced bridges that carry them over streams and gorges—no two are alike.

Don’t forget the coastal villages, from ever-popular Bar Harbor and its shingle-style and Queen Anne houses to Stonington, a working fishing town on Deer Isle. Elsewhere on Deer Isle, Edward Larrabee Barnes’s 1961 campus for the Haystack Mountain School of Crafts, an underrated masterpiece of American modernism, steps down a granite slope toward Jericho Bay, its cedar-shingled cabins and studios linked by boardwalks.

California has a little of everything, from the architectural hubs of Los Angeles and San Francisco to breathtaking natural settings. In Yosemite, El Capitan and Half Dome are jaw-dropping from the valley floor, but even more so from the top for those daring enough to make the climb. Back down in the valley, the Ahwahnee hotel, which opened in 1927, appears to be built of granite and redwood—but the “wood” is actually fireproof concrete, poured into molds and stained to look like timber. In the desert, Palm Springs is a showcase of midcentury modernism, with Richard Neutra’s 1946 Kaufmann House as its best-known example.

But the California coast is undeniably the state’s most famous landscape, and the 656 miles of Highway 1 deliver architecture along with the views. Above San Simeon, Hearst Castle, which Julia Morgan designed for William Randolph Hearst over nearly three decades, crowns a hilltop overlooking the Pacific. Continue north past the bluffs of Big Sur and storybook Carmel-by-the-Sea to the Sonoma Coast, where the redwood-clad buildings of the Sea Ranch, a planned community begun in the mid-1960s, are tucked into hedgerows to leave the meadows and bluffs open.

New York State’s famous architecture isn’t limited to the Manhattan skyline—though the city certainly pulls its weight on the architecture front. In the Adirondacks, wooded mountains surround lakes such as Lake Placid and the three Saranac Lakes. The “great camps” that wealthy families began building along their shores in the Gilded Age turned the log cabin into high style. You can still stay in one: The Point, on Upper Saranac Lake, was built in the early 1930s as Camp Wonundra for William Avery Rockefeller II and is now an 11-room Relais & Châteaux hotel, the first in North America.

In the Hudson Valley, painter Frederic Church’s hilltop villa, Olana, features a design style he called “Persian, adapted to the Occident.” The Finger Lakes offer a gentler landscape of long, narrow lakes bordered by vineyards and small towns, plus the gorge at Watkins Glen State Park, where a stone path meanders past tumbling cascades and swirling pools. And in Buffalo, you’ll find Frank Lloyd Wright’s Darwin D. Martin House, one of his finest Prairie-style designs.

The Grand Canyon is a tough act to follow, but on its South Rim, architect Mary Colter spent decades designing buildings meant to hold their own beside it. Her Hopi House, which opened in 1905, is a multistory stone building shaped like a Hopi pueblo; her Desert View Watchtower, completed in 1932, is a 70-foot stone tower modeled on Ancestral Puebloan structures, with a Snake Legend mural inside by Hopi artist Fred Kabotie.

Sedona’s red-rock buttes are spectacular on their own, but the Chapel of the Holy Cross, a modernist concrete chapel built directly into a pair of sandstone buttes and completed in 1956, gives them a focal point. North of Phoenix, Paolo Soleri’s Arcosanti, an experimental desert town of concrete domes and arches begun in 1970, is still a work in progress. And in Scottsdale, in the foothills of the McDowell Mountains, Frank Lloyd Wright’s Taliesin West—his winter home and studio from 1937 until his death in 1959—is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Texas’s landscapes range from the Chihuahuan Desert to the Gulf Coast to the bayous of Caddo Lake. In Big Bend National Park, the Chisos Mountains rise above dry plains, and the Rio Grande cuts through the narrow walls of Santa Elena Canyon. In Marfa, minimalist artist Donald Judd turned a former army post into the Chinati Foundation, a museum built around permanent, large-scale installations, including his 100 mill-aluminum boxes lined up inside two converted artillery sheds.

In Fort Worth, Louis Kahn’s Kimbell Art Museum, completed in 1972, draws architects from around the world to see natural light wash down its concrete cycloid vaults; Tadao Ando’s Modern Art Museum of Fort Worth sits just across the street. Central Texas has rolling hills, and in spring, bluebonnets and Indian paintbrush color the roadsides around Fredericksburg, a town with German heritage.

Mount Rainier is perhaps Washington’s most familiar landmark, its glaciers and snowfields visible above forests and summer wildflower meadows. The North Cascades offer even more peaks, with jagged ridges rising above turquoise Diablo Lake, while the trails in Olympic National Park lead through mossy rainforest and out to driftwood-strewn beaches.

Seattle holds its own against all that scenery. Downtown, the Central Library—designed by Rem Koolhaas’s OMA with local firm LMN and opened in 2004—wraps its stacked floors in a faceted net of glass and steel, while the Space Needle, built for the 1962 World’s Fair, remains the skyline’s signature. Outside Seattle, Port Townsend’s Victorian storefronts overlook the water, and in the Walla Walla Valley, vineyard rows and wheat fields spread across rolling hills, with the Blue Mountains rising beyond them.
